punctuated:
應天府鄉試錄序

嘉靖戊子秋八月，天下各鄉試。應天府臣先具疏以考試官請，上命臣潮、臣鐸輟講事，濫竿文柄。旣陛辭，兼程以南。比至，諸內外事咸集，而府尹臣錫實綜理加密。同考試則南曹署郎中臣民範、主事臣胤緒、臣金、臣度、評事臣以朝，奉新制也。外庠學正臣鳳、臣一溥、教諭臣國輔、臣松、臣椿、臣倫、臣晠、臣綸、訓導臣嶽，循舊典也。
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In autumn, in the eighth month of the wuzi year of Jiajing (1528), Provincial Examinations were held throughout the realm. The officials of Yingtian Prefecture first submitted a memorial requesting the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty ordered us, his servants Chao and Duo, to suspend our lecturing duties and, unworthy though we were, assume responsibility for judging literary merit [?]. After taking leave of His Majesty, we traveled south at an accelerated pace. By the time we arrived, all arrangements within and outside the examination compound were complete. The prefect, your servant Xi, had coordinated them with particular care.

The Associate Examiners appointed under the new regulations were officials of the Nanjing administration. Your servant Minfan was an Acting Bureau Director. Your servants Yinxu, Jin, and Du were Bureau Secretaries. Your servant Yichao was a Case Reviewer.

Those drawn from local Confucian schools in accordance with established precedent were as follows. Your servants Feng and Yipu were School Directors. Your servants Guofu, Song, Chun, Lun, Sheng, and Lun were Instructors. Your servant Yue was an Assistant Instructor.

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
監試則御史臣繼先臣世爵
偕入鎖院臣偕申告之曰
聖天子銳精圖治渴于求賢乃用
大臣議兩畿諸省參置京朝
之臣悉力考校且限之文體
務得眞材而罔遺滯蓋自
國朝設科以來至是益加重矣
===
吾儕其何以仰稱
德意惟公惟慎庶幾夙夜乃罔
罪愆既合提學御史臣劉隅
暨六館諸曹所簡士凡三千
一百有竒如故事三試之臣
與諸臣日夕披閲獲盡觀東
南之美瑰麗如珍竒華耀如

罪戾旣合提學御史臣劉隅
暨六館諸曹所簡士凡三千
一百有奇如故事三試之臣
與諸臣日夕披閱獲盡覩東

punctuated:
監試則御史臣繼先、臣世爵偕入鎖院。臣偕申告之曰：「聖天子銳精圖治，渴于求賢，乃用大臣議，兩畿諸省參置京朝之臣，悉力考校，且限之文體，務得眞材而罔遺滯。蓋自國朝設科以來，至是益加重矣。吾儕其何以仰稱德意？惟公惟慎，庶幾夙夜乃罔罪愆。」
既合提學御史臣劉隅暨六館諸曹所簡士，凡三千一百有竒，如故事三試之。臣與諸臣日夕披閲，獲盡觀東南之美，瑰麗如珍竒，華耀如
translation_en:
For oversight of the examination, the Censors, your servants Jixian and Shijue, entered the examination compound together and were sequestered within it. I joined in formally addressing them: “Our sagely Son of Heaven devotes his energies to good government and thirsts for worthy men. He has therefore adopted the proposal of his high ministers to include officials from the capital and court among the examiners in the two metropolitan regions and the provinces. They are to devote their full efforts to evaluating the papers, while also enforcing prescribed literary forms, determined to obtain men of true ability and leave none overlooked or held back. Since our dynasty first established the examinations, their importance has thus been further heightened. How shall we worthily fulfill his gracious intent? Only through impartiality and care may we hope, laboring day and night, to remain free of fault.”
The candidates selected by the Censor for the Supervision of Education, your servant Liu Yu, together with those selected by the six colleges and the various offices, were then assembled, numbering somewhat over three thousand one hundred. Following established practice, they were examined in three sessions. Your servant and the other officials read their papers day and night, gaining a full view of the finest talent of the southeast: magnificent as rare treasures, radiant as …

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
綺麗和適如五味其冲淡雋
永可饜飫者如嘉穀美實臣
作而言曰文其在茲乎乃擇
其精者遵
制額僅百三十有五人其不能
盡取者多矣於戲盛哉臣謹
次第名氏并錄其文以
===
獻臣惟成周賢能之書及民數
穀數皆登天府其重一也昔
禹別九州任土作貢田賦是
先其他珍產錫納無常豈非
以日用飲食有益生民國家
國所常須乎且南畿諸郡古
揚州域厥田下下漢魏以還
alt_text:
綺繡和適如五味其沖淡雋尚
永可饜飫者如嘉穀美實臣
作而言曰文其在茲乎乃擇
其精者遵
制額僅百三十有五人其不能
盡取者多矣於戲盛哉臣謹
次第名氏并錄其文以
獻臣
===
穀數皆登天府其重一也昔
禹別九州任土作貢田賦是
先其他珍產錫納無常豈非
以日用飲食有益生民國家
國所常須乎且南畿諸郡古
揚州域厥田下下漢魏以還
punctuated:
綺麗，和適如五味，其冲淡雋永可饜飫者，如嘉穀美實。臣作而言曰：「文其在茲乎！」乃擇其精者，遵制額，僅百三十有五人，其不能盡取者多矣。於戲，盛哉！臣謹次第名氏，并錄其文以獻。
臣惟成周賢能之書及民數、穀數，皆登天府，其重一也。昔禹別九州，任土作貢，田賦是先，其他珍產錫納無常，豈非以日用飲食有益生民，國家國所常須乎？且南畿諸郡，古揚州域，厥田下下，漢魏以還，
translation_en:
…splendid patterned silk, harmonious and well balanced like the five flavors; those whose unadorned subtlety and enduring savor offer full satisfaction are like fine grain and excellent fruit. Your servant rose and said: “Surely here is true literary accomplishment!” We then selected the finest, observing the prescribed quota of only 135 men; many could not be admitted. Ah, how flourishing indeed! Your servant has respectfully arranged their names in order and recorded their compositions for presentation to the throne.
Your servant reflects that under the Zhou, registers of the worthy and capable, together with population counts and grain tallies, were all deposited in the Celestial Treasury: they were accorded equal importance. Formerly, Yu divided the Nine Provinces and assessed their tribute according to the land, giving priority to levies on the fields. Other rare products were rendered as tribute without a fixed schedule. Was this not because daily food and drink benefit the people and are constantly required by the state [?]? Moreover, the prefectures of the Southern Metropolitan Region lie within ancient Yangzhou, whose fields were rated lowest of the low. From the Han and Wei onward…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
中原多事衣冠文物浸轉東
南至晋隋唐宋之間積壤流
膏號稱陸海况我
太祖高皇帝
龍飛定鼎漑植益勤我
太宗文皇帝卜世冀方匹休並重
一如甸服歳漕供御泝觀有
===
夏逺矣惟金三品瑶琨篠簜
齒革羽毛織貝橘柚之産固
所不較爾臣因是以驗
昭代才美之盛華實兼茂逺過
古昔厥亦有由哉夫自
皇祖啓配天之業及
列聖紹作人之功其開先培息非

===
夏遠矣惟金三品瑤琨篠簜
齒革羽毛織貝橘柚之產固
所不較爾臣因是以驗
昭代才美之盛華實兼茂遠過
古昔厥亦有由哉夫自
皇祖啓配天之業及
列聖紹作人之功其開先培息非
punctuated:
中原多事，衣冠文物浸轉東南。至晋隋唐宋之間，積壤流膏，號稱陸海。况我太祖高皇帝龍飛定鼎，漑植益勤；我太宗文皇帝卜世冀方，匹休並重，一如甸服，歳漕供御。泝觀有夏，逺矣！惟金三品、瑶琨、篠簜、齒革、羽毛、織貝、橘柚之産，固所不較爾。
臣因是以驗昭代才美之盛，華實兼茂，逺過古昔，厥亦有由哉！夫自皇祖啓配天之業，及列聖紹作人之功，其開先培息，非
translation_en:
…as troubles beset the Central Plain, men of rank and learning, together with the achievements of civilization, gradually shifted southeastward. By the time of the Jin, Sui, Tang, and Song dynasties, its broad lands overflowed with fertility, earning it the name “a sea on land.” All the more so when our Emperor Taizu Gao rose to imperial power and established his capital here, tending irrigation and cultivation with still greater diligence. Our Emperor Taizong Wen established the seat of his dynasty in the region of Ji; this region shared equally in its glory and importance, treated in every respect like the royal domain and annually supplying the court through grain transport by water. Tracing this back to the Xia dynasty, how far its history extends! As for its products—the three kinds of metal, precious jade, slender and large bamboo, ivory and hides, feathers and hair, patterned shells, oranges and pomelos—these assuredly cannot compare with that contribution.
From this, your servant discerns the abundance of outstanding talent in our illustrious age: refinement and substance flourish together, far surpassing antiquity. Surely this, too, has its causes! From the imperial ancestor’s inauguration of an enterprise worthy to stand alongside Heaven, through the successive sage emperors’ continuation of the work of nurturing men of talent, their pioneering and cultivation have not…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
一日矣幸際
聖明參化斂福加意元元而又
緝學崇本建極海內
萬幾之暇
躬御
宸藻闡明理道
詔示膠庠惟以敬一四箴心學
===
爲訓吁
皇極敷言之妙固作新化導之機
哉臣竊聞言從而行之則言
不可飾也行從而言之則行
不可飾也故曰君子言有物
而行有恒諸士佩服
聖化既以精切之文見錄有司則
alt_text:
一日矣幸際
聖明敘化歛福加意元元而又
緝學崇本建極海内
萬幾之暇
親御
宸藻闡明理道
詔示膠庠惟以敬一四箴心學
===
爲訓吁
皇極敷言之妙囿作新化導之機
哉臣竊聞言從而行之則言
不可飾也行從而言之則行
不可飾也故曰君子言有物
而行有恒諸士佩服
聖化旣以精切之文見録有司則
punctuated: 一日矣。幸際聖明參化斂福，加意元元，而又緝學崇本，建極海內。萬幾之暇，躬御宸藻，闡明理道，詔示膠庠，惟以敬一、四箴心學爲訓。吁！皇極敷言之妙，固作新化導之機哉！臣竊聞：言從而行之，則言不可飾也；行從而言之，則行不可飾也。故曰：「君子言有物，而行有恒。」諸士佩服聖化，既以精切之文見錄有司，則
translation_en:
…a single day. Fortunately, we live under an enlightened sage sovereign, who assists the transforming work of Heaven and Earth, gathers blessings, and gives particular care to the common people. He further advances learning and honors its foundations, establishing the supreme standard throughout the realm. Amid his myriad affairs of state, he personally takes up the imperial brush to elucidate principle and the Way, issuing instructions to the schools and teaching reverent single-mindedness and the learning of the mind embodied in the Four Admonitions. Ah! The marvel of the sovereign’s pronouncements setting forth the supreme standard is indeed the means of renewing, transforming, and guiding the people!

Your servant has humbly heard: when words are followed by action, those words cannot be mere embellishment; when actions are followed by words, those actions cannot be mere outward display. Thus it is said: “The gentleman’s words have substance, and his conduct has constancy.” These scholars have embraced Your Majesty’s sagely influence. Having been selected by the responsible officials for their precise and penetrating compositions, they then…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
亦以慤實之行施于有政先
事後食必思所以膏澤天下
如古之不忍一民之饑恥一
夫之有不獲者以無忘我
國家養賢及民之意斯聽言者
亦與有榮且以逭不明之咎
於戲士之未用恒慮不見用
===
既用矣將益考其行業不獨
以言而已則可慮者尤大也
夫致用而慮之大者實自今
日始可不慎哉臣不佞敬序
首簡且以告諸士焉
翰林院侍講學士奉直大夫
張潮謹序

亦以慤實之行施于有政先
事後食必思所以膏澤天下
如古之不忍一民之饑恥一
夫之有不獲者以無忘我
國家養賢及民之意斯聽言者
亦與有榮且以逭不明之咎
於戲士之未用恒慮不見用
===
既用矣將益考其行業不獨
以言而已則可慮者尤大也
夫致用而慮之大者實自今
日始可不慎哉臣不佞敬序
首簡且以告諸士焉
翰林院侍講學士奉直大夫
張潮謹序
punctuated:
亦以慤實之行施于有政，先事後食，必思所以膏澤天下，如古之不忍一民之饑、恥一夫之有不獲者，以無忘我國家養賢及民之意。斯聽言者亦與有榮，且以逭不明之咎。於戲！士之未用，恒慮不見用；既用矣，將益考其行業，不獨以言而已，則可慮者尤大也。夫致用而慮之大者，實自今日始，可不慎哉？臣不佞，敬序首簡，且以告諸士焉。
翰林院侍講學士、奉直大夫張潮謹序。
translation_en:
…they should likewise bring sincere and substantial conduct to the administration of government, putting service before remuneration. They must consider how to confer benefits upon all under Heaven, like the ancients who could not bear that a single person should go hungry and felt shame if even one man failed to receive his due. Thus they will not forget our dynasty’s intention in nurturing worthy men so that its benefits may reach the people. Then those who judge men by their words will also share in the honor and escape the blame of having lacked discernment.
Alas! Before scholars are employed, they constantly worry that they will not be employed. Once employed, their conduct and achievements will be examined still more closely, and they will no longer be judged by words alone. Their grounds for concern are therefore greater still. Indeed, the grave concerns attendant upon being put to service begin this very day. Can they fail to be vigilant? Your untalented servant respectfully writes this preface at the beginning of the volume, also to convey this admonition to the scholars.
Preface respectfully composed by Zhang Chao, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Upright Service.

Examiners

Zhang Chao, Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Straightforward Service. His courtesy name was Weixin; he was from Neijiang County, Sichuan, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinwei year.

Peng Ze, Grand Master for Deliberation and Right Exhorter of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent. His courtesy name was Renqing; he was from Nanhai County, Guangdong, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingchou year.

Yu Yinxu, Gentleman for Straightforward Service and Secretary of the Sichuan Bureau in the Nanjing Ministry of Revenue. His courtesy name was Sixiao; he was from Yingcheng County, Huguang, and was a metropolitan graduate of an illegible year (□□).

Qin Jin, Gentleman for Straightforward Service and Secretary of the Huguang Bureau in the Nanjing Ministry of Justice. His courtesy name was Guosheng; he was registered in Linhai County, Zhejiang, and was originally from Changshu. He was a metropolitan graduate of an illegible year (□□).

Wang Du, Gentleman for Straightforward Service and Secretary of the Bureau of State Farms in the Nanjing Ministry of Works. His courtesy name was Lüsheng; he was registered in Linhai County, Zhejiang, and was originally from Changshu. He was a metropolitan graduate of the guiwei year.

Jiang Yichao, Left Case Reviewer of the Left Office of the Nanjing Court of Judicial Review. His courtesy name was Yuchun; he was from Guixi County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the bingxu year.

Yang Feng, Instructor at the Confucian School of Shanzhou, Henan Prefecture, Henan. His courtesy name was Mingrui; he was from Macheng County, Huguang, and was a tribute student (gongshi) of the jimao year.

Qian Yuan, Instructor at the Confucian School of Junzhou, Xiangyang Prefecture, Huguang. His courtesy name was Kexue; he was from Shanyin County, Zhejiang, and was a tribute student of the jimao year.

Lin Guofu, Instructor at the Confucian School of Jinhua County, Jinhua Prefecture, Zhejiang. His courtesy name was Sizhen; he was from Putian County, Fujian, and was a tribute student of the renwu year.

Cao Song, Instructor at the Confucian School of Songxi County, Jianning Prefecture, Fujian. His courtesy name was Tingjie; he was from Fuliang County, Jiangxi, and was a tribute student of the bingzi year.

Lin Chun, Instructor at the Confucian School of Fenyi County, Yuanzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Yongnian; he was from Houguan County, Fujian, and was a tribute student of the jimao year.

Pan Lun, Instructor at the Confucian School of Jianyang County, Jianning Prefecture, Fujian. His courtesy name was Gongxu; he was from Gaoyao County, Guangdong, and was a tribute student of the renwu year.

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
殷因於夏禮所損益可知也周因於殷禮
所損益可知也
柔遠人則四方歸之懷諸侯則天下畏之
成覸謂齊景公曰彼丈夫也我丈夫也吾
何畏彼哉顔淵曰舜何人也予何人也
有爲者亦若是公明儀曰文王我師也
周公豈欺我哉
易
知終終之可與存義也
渙有丘匪夷所思
通乎晝夜之道而知
化而裁之存乎變推而行之存乎通神而
明之存乎其人黙而成之不言而信存
乎德行
書
予違汝弼汝無面從退有後言欽四鄰

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

殷因於夏禮，所損益可知也；周因於殷禮，所損益可知也。

柔遠人，則四方歸之；懷諸侯，則天下畏之。

成覸謂齊景公曰：「彼丈夫也，我丈夫也，吾何畏彼哉？」顔淵曰：「舜何人也？予何人也？有爲者亦若是。」公明儀曰：「文王，我師也，周公豈欺我哉？」

易

知終終之，可與存義也。

渙有丘，匪夷所思。

通乎晝夜之道而知。

化而裁之存乎變，推而行之存乎通，神而明之存乎其人，黙而成之、不言而信存乎德行。

書

予違，汝弼；汝無面從，退有後言。欽四鄰。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Yin followed the rites of the Xia; what they diminished and added can be known. The Zhou followed the rites of the Yin; what they diminished and added can be known.

Treat people from afar with kindness, and those from the four quarters will turn to you; cherish the feudal lords, and all under Heaven will stand in awe of you.

Cheng Jian said to Duke Jing of Qi: “He is a man, and I am a man. Why should I fear him?” Yan Yuan said: “What sort of person was Shun? What sort of person am I? Anyone who strives to accomplish something can likewise become such a person.” Gongming Yi said: “‘King Wen is my teacher’—could the Duke of Zhou have deceived me?”

Book of Changes

Knowing when to end and bringing matters to their proper end, one can help preserve righteousness.

Amid dispersion there is a gathering like a mound—something beyond ordinary thought.

Comprehending the Way of day and night, he understands.

Transforming and regulating things depends on change; extending and putting them into practice depends on free passage. Making their spiritual efficacy manifest depends on the right person; accomplishing things silently and inspiring trust without words depends on virtuous conduct.

Book of Documents

If I err, you must correct me. Do not agree with me to my face and then speak against me after withdrawing. Be reverent, you who stand around me on all four sides.

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
惟后非賢不乂惟賢非后不食其爾克紹
乃辟于先王永綏民
平康正直彊弗友剛克燮友柔克沉潛剛
克高明柔克
爾尚式時周公之猷訓惟日孜孜無敢逸
豫
詩
被之僮僮夙夜在公被之祁祁薄言還歸
君子萬年介爾遐福
===
媚茲一人應侯順德永言孝思昭哉嗣服
鼗鼓淵淵嘒嘒管聲既和且平依我磬聲
於赫湯孫穆穆厥聲庸鼓有斁萬舞有
奕我有嘉客亦不夷懌
春秋
三月鄭伯使宛來歸祊庚寅我入祊〔隱公八年〕
鄭伯以璧假許田〔桓公元年〕
春王三月甲寅齊人伐衛衛人及齊人戰
衛人敗績〔莊公二十八年〕

衛人敗績〔莊公二十八年〕
punctuated:
惟后非賢不乂，惟賢非后不食。其爾克紹乃辟于先王，永綏民。
平康正直，彊弗友剛克，燮友柔克，沉潛剛克，高明柔克。
爾尚式時周公之猷訓，惟日孜孜，無敢逸豫。

詩
被之僮僮，夙夜在公；被之祁祁，薄言還歸。
君子萬年，介爾遐福。
媚茲一人，應侯順德。永言孝思，昭哉嗣服！
鼗鼓淵淵，嘒嘒管聲。既和且平，依我磬聲。於赫湯孫，穆穆厥聲。庸鼓有斁，萬舞有奕。我有嘉客，亦不夷懌？

春秋
三月，鄭伯使宛來歸祊。庚寅，我入祊。〔隱公八年〕
鄭伯以璧假許田。〔桓公元年〕
春，王三月，甲寅，齊人伐衛。衛人及齊人戰，衛人敗績。〔莊公二十八年〕
translation_en:
Without worthy men, a ruler cannot govern; without a ruler, worthy men cannot receive sustenance. May you enable your sovereign to carry on the legacy of the former kings and bring lasting peace to the people.
In peaceful and settled times, govern with uprightness. Subdue the strong and uncompliant with firmness, and the harmonious and compliant with gentleness. Deal with the withdrawn and reserved through firmness, and with the lofty and brilliant through gentleness.
May you follow these counsels and instructions of the Duke of Zhou, applying yourself diligently each day, never daring to indulge in ease or pleasure.

Book of Odes
Her headdress is stately; early and late she attends to public duties. Her headdress is graceful; now she returns home.
May the lord live ten thousand years; may great and enduring blessings be bestowed upon you.
Love this one man, the sovereign, and respond to his compliant virtue. Ever cherish filial thoughts: glorious is his succession to office!
The pellet drums and great drums resound deeply; the pipes sound clear and shrill. Harmonious and balanced, they follow the sound of our chime stones. Ah, illustrious descendant of Tang! How solemn is the music! The great bells and drums sound abundantly; the wan dance is splendid. We have honored guests: are they not at ease and delighted?

Spring and Autumn Annals
In the third month, the Earl of Zheng sent Wan to return Beng to us. On the gengyin day, we entered Beng. 〔Eighth year of Duke Yin〕
The Earl of Zheng used a jade disc to obtain the use of the fields of Xu. 〔First year of Duke Huan〕
In spring, in the third month of the royal calendar, on the jiayin day, the men of Qi attacked Wei. The men of Wei fought the men of Qi, and the men of Wei suffered a crushing defeat. 〔Twenty-eighth year of Duke Zhuang〕

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
丁亥楚子入陳宣公十一年楚子圍鄭宣
公十二年
晋伐鮮虞昭公十二年吳伐我哀公八年
禮記
百官各以其成質於三官大司徒大司馬
大司空以百官之成質於天子百官齊
戒受質
故經禮三百曲禮三千其致一也未有入
室而不由戶者君子之於禮也有所竭
===
情盡慎致其敬而誠若有美而文而誠
若
寬裕肉好順成和動之音作而民慈愛
夫孝置之而塞乎天地溥之而橫乎四海
施諸後世而無朝夕

丁亥，楚子入陳。宣公十一年。楚子圍鄭。宣公十二年。
晋伐鮮虞。昭公十二年。吳伐我。哀公八年。
禮記
百官各以其成質於三官，大司徒、大司馬、大司空以百官之成質於天子，百官齊戒受質。
故經禮三百，曲禮三千，其致一也。未有入室而不由戶者。君子之於禮也，有所竭情盡慎，致其敬而誠若；有美而文而誠若。
寬裕肉好、順成和動之音作，而民慈愛。
夫孝，置之而塞乎天地，溥之而橫乎四海，施諸後世而無朝夕。
第貳場
論
聖人能立無過之地。
詔誥表內科一道。
translation_en:
On the dinghai day, the Viscount of Chu entered Chen. Eleventh year of Duke Xuan. The Viscount of Chu besieged Zheng. Twelfth year of Duke Xuan.
Jin attacked Xianyu. Twelfth year of Duke Zhao. Wu attacked us [Lu]. Eighth year of Duke Ai.
Book of Rites (Liji)
The hundred officials each submit their completed work for assessment to the three ministers. The Minister of Education, Minister of War, and Minister of Works submit the completed work of the hundred officials to the Son of Heaven for assessment. The hundred officials purify themselves and observe abstinence to receive the assessment.
Thus there are three hundred principal rites and three thousand detailed rules of propriety, yet their ultimate purport is one. No one has ever entered a room without passing through its doorway. In his practice of ritual, the gentleman sometimes pours out his feelings, exercises the utmost care, and expresses his reverence with sincerity; sometimes he displays beauty and refinement, likewise with sincerity.
When music that is expansive and unhurried, full and pleasing, orderly in its development and harmonious in its movement is played, the people become compassionate and loving.
As for filial piety, set it in place and it fills heaven and earth; spread it abroad and it extends across the Four Seas; apply it to later generations and it holds at all times, morning and evening alike.
Second Session
Discourse
The sage can establish himself in a position free from error.
One question from among edicts, proclamations, and memorials [科 is doubtful here].

translation_en:
Compose an edict in the voice of a Han emperor establishing additional Erudites for the three classics: the Book of Changes, the Book of Documents, and the Spring and Autumn Annals. 〔Ganlu〕〔third year〕
Compose an edict in the voice of a Tang emperor appointing Li Jing as Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs. 〔Fourth year of Zhenguan〕
Compose a memorial in the voice of the Song Hanlin Reader-in-waiting Yan Shu and his colleagues, requesting that the emperor attend instruction within the palace during the summer months. 〔Eighth year of Tiansheng〕
Legal judgments 〔five items〕: Unauthorized establishment of official posts and clerical positions; allowing farmland to lie waste; clothing and dwellings that violate prescribed standards; preferential relief for military dependents; illicitly breaching river defenses.
Third Session
Policy questions 〔five questions〕
Question: From antiquity, emperors and kings have all used rites and music to transform and perfect the realm. Yet no music surpassed the Shao dance in splendor, and no rites were more complete than those of the Zhou at its height. Was this because emperors and kings could not equal one another? Or, from the Three Dynasties onward, how were their institutions created, inherited, and altered? We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao used the ways of the Chinese to transform the barbarians and swept clean the realm within the seas. The grandeur of his rites and music …

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同天地其本諸身心達之天下者雖古
帝王莫加焉而漢唐宋不足言矣亦可
鋪張揚厲之歟且
御極之初首開禮樂二局徵天下耆儒宿學
講求參訂既又命官分掌典章文物彬
彬如也今所輯禮儀諸書傳布已久惟
樂律之制未有纂述俾天下誦習而歌
舞之竊聞
聖祖嘗曰古之律呂協天地自然之氣後世律
===
呂出人爲智巧之私
宸慮淵微固未易測然莊誦
祖訓
大誥二書首以慎兵刑造福正倫爲急他日
閱漢史又深惜孝文令主不能因時損益以
復三代之舊
聖謨宏遠豈非有待而然歟今我
皇上禀聖神之資乘熈洽之運奉
天勤民惇典敬德善繼善述兹其時矣諸生其

鋪張揚厲之歟且
御極之初首開禮樂二局徵天下耆儒宿學
講求參訂既又命官分掌典章文物彬彬
彬如也今所輯禮儀諸書傳布已久惟
樂律之制未有纂述俾天下誦習而歌
舞之竊聞
皇祖嘗曰古之律呂協天地自然之氣後世律
呂出人爲智巧之私
宸慮淵微固未易測然莊誦
===
祖訓
大誥二書首以慎兵刑造福正倫爲急他日
閱漢史又深惜孝文令主不能因時損益以
復三代之舊
聖謨宏遠豈非有待而然歟今我
皇上禀聖神之資乘熈洽之運奉
天勤民惇典敬德善繼善述茲其時矣諸生其
punctuated: 同天地，其本諸身心、達之天下者，雖古帝王莫加焉，而漢唐宋不足言矣，亦可鋪張揚厲之歟？且御極之初，首開禮樂二局，徵天下耆儒宿學，講求參訂。既又命官分掌，典章文物彬彬如也。今所輯禮儀諸書，傳布已久，惟樂律之制未有纂述，俾天下誦習而歌舞之。竊聞聖祖嘗曰：「古之律呂，協天地自然之氣；後世律呂，出人爲智巧之私。」宸慮淵微，固未易測。然莊誦《祖訓》《大誥》二書，首以慎兵刑、造福、正倫爲急。他日閱漢史，又深惜孝文令主不能因時損益，以復三代之舊。聖謨宏遠，豈非有待而然歟？今我皇上禀聖神之資，乘熈洽之運，奉天勤民，惇典敬德，善繼善述，兹其時矣。諸生其
translation_en: …matches Heaven and Earth. What he grounded in his own person and mind and extended throughout the realm could not be surpassed even by the emperors and kings of antiquity; the Han, Tang, and Song scarcely merit mention. Might you also set forth and extol these achievements? Moreover, at the beginning of his reign, he first established the two bureaus for ritual and music, summoning venerable Confucian scholars and seasoned men of learning from throughout the realm to investigate, compare, and settle their provisions. He then appointed officials to take separate charge, and institutions and cultural accomplishments flourished in elegant harmony. The books on ritual and ceremony compiled at that time have long circulated, but the system of musical pitches alone has yet to be compiled and expounded so that all under Heaven may recite and study it and perform its songs and dances. We have respectfully heard that the sagely founder once said: “The pitch standards of antiquity accorded with the natural vital energies of Heaven and Earth; those of later ages arose from the private contrivances of human ingenuity.” The imperial thought was profound and subtle, and certainly not easy to fathom. Yet, when we reverently recite the Ancestral Instructions and the Great Pronouncements, these two books give foremost urgency to caution in warfare and punishments, bringing blessings to the people, and setting human relationships right. On another occasion, while reading the history of the Han, he deeply regretted that Emperor Xiaowen, an excellent ruler, had failed to make additions and reductions suited to his times and thereby restore the ancient institutions of the Three Dynasties. His sagely plans were vast and far-reaching: was this not because he awaited their future fulfillment? Now our Emperor possesses sagely and divine gifts and reigns in an age of prosperity and concord. He serves Heaven, labors for the people, upholds the enduring norms, and reveres virtue. This is indeed the time to carry forward his predecessor’s undertakings and fulfill his intentions. You candidates should…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
悉古今之蘊敬著于篇為
聖孝萬一之助
問天人相為流通感應之際不可誣也乃
稽載籍則若有可疑者試相與論之災
祥之說並見于經春秋何以不書慶祥
漢儒通陰陽之理以陳時事者衆矣春
秋何以不著事應堯湯大聖水旱不免
而麟鳳龜龍之出歐陽氏且力辨之然
河圖洛書非瑞歟至鄭夾漈則又疑于
===
五行之說何也文景漢之令主災異頻
仍無損于治而武宣之世芝房寶鼎神
爵甘露至形于歌詠或以改元其與龍
師鳥官儀鳳嘉禾之紀有不同歟開元
咸平非不抑祥瑞後乃致天寶祥符之
紛紛其何故歟
皇上臨御以來厲精圖治允協
天心邇者郡國上河清甘露之瑞
詔勿稱賀一遇水旱風霾之異則

punctuated:
悉古今之蘊，敬著于篇，為聖孝萬一之助。

問：天人相為流通，感應之際不可誣也。乃稽載籍，則若有可疑者，試相與論之。災祥之說並見于經，《春秋》何以不書慶祥？漢儒通陰陽之理以陳時事者衆矣，《春秋》何以不著事應？堯湯大聖，水旱不免，而麟鳳龜龍之出，歐陽氏且力辨之。然河圖洛書非瑞歟？至鄭夾漈，則又疑于五行之說，何也？文景，漢之令主，災異頻仍，無損于治；而武宣之世，芝房、寶鼎、神爵、甘露，至形于歌詠，或以改元，其與龍師、鳥官、儀鳳、嘉禾之紀有不同歟？開元、咸平非不抑祥瑞，後乃致天寶、祥符之紛紛，其何故歟？皇上臨御以來，厲精圖治，允協天心。邇者郡國上河清、甘露之瑞，詔勿稱賀。一遇水旱風霾之異，則
translation_en:
…fully set forth the profound meaning of past and present, respectfully committing it to writing, to offer even the slightest assistance to His Majesty’s sagely filial devotion.

Question: Heaven and humanity communicate with one another; their mutual influence and response cannot be denied. Yet when we examine the written records, certain points seem doubtful. Let us discuss them. Accounts of calamities and auspicious signs both appear in the Classics. Why does the Spring and Autumn Annals not record auspicious occurrences? Many Han scholars drew upon the principles of yin and yang to discuss contemporary affairs. Why does the Spring and Autumn Annals not explicitly identify events and their corresponding portents? Yao and Tang were great sages, yet they could not escape floods and droughts. Master Ouyang, moreover, vigorously disputed accounts of the appearance of qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and dragons. But were the River Chart and the Luo Writing not auspicious signs? As for Zheng Jiaji, he also questioned the theory of the Five Phases. Why was this?

Emperors Wen and Jing were worthy rulers of the Han. Calamities and anomalies occurred repeatedly, yet did not impair their good government. Under Emperors Wu and Xuan, however, the hall of numinous mushrooms, the precious tripod, divine birds, and sweet dew were even celebrated in songs, and some prompted changes of era name. Did these differ from the records of dragon-named and bird-named officials, phoenixes appearing in stately array, and auspicious grain? During the Kaiyuan and Xianping eras, efforts were indeed made to discourage the celebration of auspicious signs. Why, then, did these give way to the profusion of such affairs during the Tianbao and Xiangfu eras?

Since His Majesty ascended the throne, he has devoted his energies to achieving good government, truly according with Heaven’s intent. Recently, local administrations reported the auspicious signs of the Yellow River running clear and sweet dew, but he decreed that no congratulations should be offered. Whenever anomalous floods, droughts, winds, or dust haze occur, then…

問：周禮一書，周公致太平之跡也。昔人指之爲經，而禮記爲傳。今傳與諸經並行，而是書疑者紛紛不一。或謂成於既黜殷命之際，或謂作於既營成周之後。以今攷之，果於何時？書何從而始出，抑何人而後傳？周禮、周官何自而分？博士學官何故不列？分土何以異於王制？班爵何以不合軻書？考工記果足以續冬官？五官中果何見其殘闕？設官分職何數倍於周官？遂人、匠人何不同於溝洫？內宰之掌有不可通者三，三物之法有不能行者三。屬民讀法近於擾，廛人五布近於苛，國服爲息近於利。載師何以及
translation_en:
…he issues instructions to his assembled ministers that they all cultivate themselves and examine their conduct. This is precisely the anxious diligence and vigilant self-discipline of the ancient sage kings. Although we cherish humble offerings—as of celery or the warmth of the sun—we have no occasion to present them. Moreover, we have repeatedly sought the underlying causes of calamities and auspicious signs, but have yet to grasp them. When discussion reaches a matter and one does not speak, this is called concealment. We ask that you state your views forthrightly, so that they may be conveyed to His Majesty.
Question: The Rites of Zhou is a record of how the Duke of Zhou brought about Great Peace. Earlier scholars designated it a classic and the Record of Rites its commentary. Today the commentary circulates alongside the other classics, yet doubts about this book are numerous and varied. Some say it was completed just after the mandate of Yin had been revoked; others say it was composed after Chengzhou had been built. Examining the matter now, when exactly was it written? From where did the book first emerge, and through whom was it subsequently transmitted? How did the titles Rites of Zhou and Offices of Zhou come to be distinguished? Why are erudites and educational officials not listed? Why does its allocation of territory differ from that in the “Royal Regulations”? Why does its distribution of noble ranks disagree with the book of Meng Ke? Can the Record of Artificers truly serve as a continuation of the Offices of Winter? What evidence of omissions and losses can actually be found in the other five offices? Why does the number of offices established and duties assigned exceed several times over that in the “Offices of Zhou” chapter of the Book of Documents? Why do the Directors of Outlying Districts and the master builders differ in their provisions for drainage channels? There are three incomprehensible points in the duties of the Palace Steward, and three impracticable points in the system of the three categories of instruction. Assembling the people to read out the laws verges on harassment; the five levies of the Market Officers verge on excessive exaction; taking service to the state as interest verges on seeking profit. title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
干賈田賓客何以屬于司寇玉府内府
供貢之非執璧致飮屈伸之亂甚則内
小臣掌好命於四方媒氏男女奔者不
之禁尤爲傷悖之極皆吾儒舊所未信
安得無十論七難之排六國陰謀之詆
而行之者一敗於新室再敗於熙寧爲
惑所以滋甚也或以爲非周全書而秦
漢諸儒多所損益者歟抑思兼不合故
於夏商岐周之制更有所斟酌歟豈孟
===
氏之所未見而漢人乃得以表章之歟
探本伺末之說不無穿鑿之甚歟然隋
之名儒慕其爲王道之極唐之英主嘆
其爲眞聖作者是豈無所據歟抑信之
篤乃所以過致其疑歟夫聖人之經未
敢輕議而朱子爲世大儒攷據精詳凡
所論著不一而足其必有以折衷者矣
請致析于篇以觀究心之學
問知人難矣知而薦之以登於用不愈難

干賈田？賓客何以屬于司寇？玉府、内府供貢之非，執璧致飮屈伸之亂，甚則内小臣掌好命於四方，媒氏男女奔者不之禁，尤爲傷悖之極，皆吾儒舊所未信。安得無十論七難之排、六國陰謀之詆？而行之者，一敗於新室，再敗於熙寧，爲惑所以滋甚也。或以爲非周全書，而秦漢諸儒多所損益者歟？抑思兼不合，故於夏商岐周之制更有所斟酌歟？豈孟氏之所未見，而漢人乃得以表章之歟？探本伺末之說，不無穿鑿之甚歟？然隋之名儒慕其爲王道之極，唐之英主嘆其爲眞聖作者，是豈無所據歟？抑信之篤，乃所以過致其疑歟？夫聖人之經未敢輕議，而朱子爲世大儒，攷據精詳，凡所論著不一而足，其必有以折衷者矣。請致析于篇，以觀究心之學。
問：知人難矣，知而薦之以登於用，不愈難
translation_en:
…interfere with merchants’ fields [?]? Why are guests placed under the Minister of Justice? There are improprieties in the supplies and tribute furnished by the Jade Treasury and Inner Treasury, and confusion concerning the holding of jade tablets, the offering of drink, and the gestures of deference and precedence. More seriously, the Minor Palace Attendants administer messages of goodwill to the four quarters, while the Matchmaker does not prohibit men and women from eloping. These are especially flagrant violations of propriety, all matters that our Confucian scholars have long found unworthy of belief. How could there fail to be attacks such as the “Ten Arguments” and “Seven Objections,” or the denunciation that this was a conspiracy of the Six States? Moreover, attempts to implement it failed first under the Xin dynasty and again during the Xining reign period. This has only deepened the doubts.
Perhaps it is not an intact book from the Zhou, but one to which scholars of the Qin and Han made numerous additions and deletions? Or was there an intention to combine incompatible elements [?], and consequently to make further adjustments among the institutions of the Xia, Shang, and the Zhou at Qi? Could it be that the Han scholars succeeded in bringing to light what Mengzi had never seen? Might the explanations that trace its origins and investigate its later development themselves involve excessive forced interpretation?
Yet a renowned scholar of the Sui admired it as the supreme expression of the Kingly Way, and an illustrious Tang ruler praised it as truly the work of a sage. Could these judgments have had no foundation? Or was it precisely profound faith in it that gave rise to excessive doubt? We dare not lightly criticize a classic of the sages. Master Zhu, however, was a great Confucian scholar of his age, meticulous and thorough in his textual investigations. His discussions and writings on the subject are too numerous to enumerate; surely they provide a basis for a balanced judgment. Please set out a detailed analysis in your essay, so that we may assess the learning you have devoted to this inquiry.
Question: To judge men is difficult. Having judged them, is it not still more difficult to recommend them for appointment…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
乎守一節者慮未善其後敦久要者慮
或變其初不知所謂郡守公府皆得舉
士直指金吾咸可薦賢其能無誤否也
況如王介甫過信惠卿呂微仲首引楊
畏豈直貽一身之戚將以釀國家無窮
之憂不亦大可懼乎然嘗聞晏元獻之
與范文正一問答之閒而萃四相張忠
定之與范延貴一邂逅之頃而發二士
似甚易易焉者不知以何為取人之則
===
也又如君辱臣死嘗自叙卑矣有違衆舉
之亦成一匡之功剛褊有名非汪度矣
有矯俗薦之竟著澶淵之烈若是取材
又與常情異者將用其長而略其短歟
抑論人者當以大節為先歟或時之所
需於材有相宜不暇計其他歟昔人謂
於不巳若者不比之一聞人過終身不
忘為不可以理國何邇來羣議乃大異
於是歟一時士習之趨嚮所係亦甚重

忘為不可以理國何邇來羣議乃大異
於是歟一時士習之趨嚮所係亦甚□
punctuated: 乎？守一節者，慮未善其後；敦久要者，慮或變其初。不知所謂郡守、公府皆得舉士，直指、金吾咸可薦賢，其能無誤否也？況如王介甫過信惠卿，呂微仲首引楊畏，豈直貽一身之戚，將以釀國家無窮之憂，不亦大可懼乎？然嘗聞晏元獻之與范文正，一問答之閒而萃四相；張忠定之與范延貴，一邂逅之頃而發二士，似甚易易焉者。不知以何為取人之則也？又如君辱臣死，嘗自叙卑矣，有違衆舉之，亦成一匡之功；剛褊有名，非汪度矣，有矯俗薦之，竟著澶淵之烈。若是取材，又與常情異者，將用其長而略其短歟？抑論人者當以大節為先歟？或時之所需，於材有相宜，不暇計其他歟？昔人謂於不巳若者不比之，一聞人過終身不忘，為不可以理國。何邇來羣議乃大異於是歟？一時士習之趨嚮，所係亦甚重
translation_en:
…is it not still more difficult? With someone who holds fast to a particular principle, one worries that he may not maintain his conduct to the end; with someone devoted to old commitments, one worries that he may depart from his original intentions. Under the arrangements whereby prefects and the offices of the highest dignitaries could all nominate scholars, and investigating censors and officers of the Imperial Insignia Guard could all recommend worthy men, could mistakes really be avoided? Consider, moreover, Wang Jiefu’s excessive trust in Huiqing, or Lü Weizhong’s initial sponsorship of Yang Wei. These brought more than personal sorrow: they would brew endless troubles for the state. Is this not greatly to be feared?
Yet we have heard that a single exchange between Yan Yuanxian and Fan Wenzheng brought together four future chief councillors, and that a chance encounter between Zhang Zhongding and Fan Yangui brought two worthy men to light. These cases seem exceedingly easy. What standard did they use in selecting men?
Again, there was the man who, by the principle that a minister should die when his lord is humiliated, had once acknowledged his own low standing [?]; someone nevertheless nominated him against general opinion, and he accomplished the task of setting the realm right. Another was notorious for his obstinacy and narrowness, scarcely a man of generous breadth; someone nevertheless recommended him against prevailing opinion, and he ultimately achieved distinction at Chanyuan. Such selections of talent also depart from ordinary judgments. Were their strengths to be employed and their shortcomings overlooked? Or should the assessment of men give priority to their conduct in matters of great consequence? Or did their abilities suit the needs of the time, leaving no leisure to reckon with anything else?
An earlier writer said that someone who would not associate with those inferior to himself [?], and who, once he heard of another’s fault, never forgot it for the rest of his life, could not govern a state. Why, then, has collective opinion lately diverged so greatly from this view? The direction taken by the habits of scholars in any age has consequences of very great importance…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
焉如何而盡明揚之道如何而得變動
之機願聞其說
問真西山讀史嘗載吕氏之言曰當漢之
治用人必先曰長者舉事必先曰大體
其人若事可指而言歟且獨謂漢何也
夷考其時風移俗易吏稱民安要之不
爲無自及觀洛陽太息之書膠東勞來
之詔則又有異焉者可得聞其故歟我
朝垂百六十年于兹紀綱正于上風俗厚于
===
下區區漢治不足言矣顧承平日久漸
以玩弊吏或苛細而少循良之風士或
憸邪而寡廉靜之節貴賤或踰而訟訐
者無已兵將或驕而猖狂者不戢此有
識者不能無隱憂也今思所以通變之
術必用皆得人而事合體要其何以行
之求之前代亦或類是而有可法者乎
願毋諱焉以觀平居用世之志

朝垂百六十年于茲紀綱正于上風俗厚于
===
下區區漢治不足言矣顧承平日久漸
以玩弊吏或苛細而少循良之風士或
憸邪而寡廉靜之節貴賤或踰而訟訐
者無已兵將或驕而倡狂者不戢此有
識者不能無隱憂也今思所以通變之
術必用皆得人而事合體要其何以行
之求之前代亦或類是而有可法者乎
願毋諱焉以觀平居用世之志
punctuated:
焉。如何而盡明揚之道？如何而得變動之機？願聞其說。

問：真西山讀史，嘗載吕氏之言曰：「當漢之治，用人必先曰長者，舉事必先曰大體。」其人若事，可指而言歟？且獨謂漢，何也？夷考其時，風移俗易，吏稱民安，要之不爲無自。及觀洛陽太息之書、膠東勞來之詔，則又有異焉者，可得聞其故歟？我朝垂百六十年于兹，紀綱正于上，風俗厚于下，區區漢治不足言矣。顧承平日久，漸以玩弊，吏或苛細而少循良之風，士或憸邪而寡廉靜之節，貴賤或踰而訟訐者無已，兵將或驕而猖狂者不戢，此有識者不能無隱憂也。今思所以通變之術，必用皆得人，而事合體要，其何以行之？求之前代，亦或類是而有可法者乎？願毋諱焉，以觀平居用世之志。
translation_en:
…How can the way of recognizing and promoting worthy men be fully realized? How can the opportunity for change be grasped? I wish to hear your explanation.

Question: Zhen Xishan, in his reading of history, once recorded Master Lü’s words: “Under Han rule, in appointing men, the first consideration was always whether they were men of mature virtue; in undertaking affairs, the first consideration was always the larger principles.” Can you identify and discuss the men and affairs concerned? And why did he speak specifically of the Han? Upon examining that age, we find that prevailing ways and customs were transformed, officials won praise, and the people enjoyed peace. These things surely had their causes. Yet when we read the memorial of deep sighs by the man of Luoyang and the edict concerning solicitude for and encouragement of the people of Jiaodong, a different picture emerges. May we hear the reasons for this?

Our dynasty has now endured for nearly a hundred and sixty years. The guiding principles of government are properly ordered above, and the customs of the people are sound below. The modest achievements of Han government scarcely merit mention. Yet prolonged peace has gradually brought laxity and abuses. Some officials are harsh and meddlesome, with little of the spirit of conscientious and benevolent administration; some scholars are unscrupulous and perverse, lacking integrity and restraint. Distinctions between high and low are sometimes transgressed, and litigation and mutual accusations have no end. Soldiers and commanders sometimes grow arrogant, and their reckless behavior goes unchecked. Those with discernment cannot but harbor private anxiety over this.

If we now consider methods of adapting to changed circumstances, so that every appointment secures the right man and every undertaking accords with essential principles, how should these methods be put into practice? If we look to earlier dynasties, were there comparable circumstances that might offer examples to follow? Please speak without reserve, so that we may see the aspirations for public service that you have cultivated in your everyday lives.

text:
此意謂世不能外禮以爲治亦不能外綱常以
爲禮三綱天所叙也五常天所命也故殷繼夏
而王嘗因之而不變矣非不變也道之所在不
可得而變也然或裁其有餘或補其不足亦斟
酌其會通品節乎典禮者爾如忠質之異尚也
寅丑之迭建也雖杞宋無徵吾嘗學之而能言
之有不可知者乎周繼殷而王亦因之而不變
矣非不變也以本乎道自不容于變也然過者
則損之不及則益之亦變通以趨時中而已如
===
以者爾如質易而文也丑易而子也今方策具
存吾嘗學之而固從之有不可知者乎因往推
來百世從可知已抑夫子爲下不倍故曰吾從
周其弊也則欲從先進而有志三代之英故惓
惓致意焉惜乎有德無位爾雖然斯禮之在萬
世如一日垂訓之功大矣哉
柔遠人則四方歸之懷諸侯則天下畏之
蔣信

此意，謂世不能外禮以爲治，亦不能外綱常以爲禮。三綱，天所叙也；五常，天所命也。故殷繼夏而王，嘗因之而不變矣。非不變也，道之所在，不可得而變也。然或裁其有餘，或補其不足，亦斟酌其會通，品節乎典禮者爾。如忠質之異尚也，寅丑之迭建也，雖杞宋無徵，吾嘗學之而能言之，有不可知者乎？周繼殷而王，亦因之而不變矣。非不變也，以本乎道，自不容于變也。然過者則損之，不及則益之，亦變通以趨時中而已。如以者爾，如質易而文也，丑易而子也。今方策具存，吾嘗學之而固從之，有不可知者乎？因往推來，百世從可知已。抑夫子爲下不倍，故曰「吾從周」。其弊也，則欲從先進，而有志三代之英，故惓惓致意焉。惜乎有德無位爾！雖然，斯禮之在，萬世如一日，垂訓之功大矣哉！

柔遠人則四方歸之，懷諸侯則天下畏之。
蔣信

translation_en:
…this meaning: that no age can govern apart from ritual, nor can it establish ritual apart from the cardinal bonds and constant virtues. The Three Bonds are ordered by Heaven; the Five Constant Virtues are ordained by Heaven. Thus, when the Yin succeeded the Xia as kings, they inherited these without changing them. It was not merely that they did not change them: where the Way resides, change is impossible. Yet they sometimes curtailed what was excessive or supplemented what was insufficient, simply weighing how institutions could be adapted and brought into accord, and regulating the ceremonial rites accordingly. Examples include their different preferences for loyalty and simplicity, and the successive designation of the months associated with yin and chou as the beginning of the year. Although Qi and Song offer insufficient evidence, I have studied these matters and can speak of them. Is there anything that cannot be known?

When the Zhou succeeded the Yin as kings, they too inherited these without changing them. It was not merely that they did not change them: because these were rooted in the Way, they inherently admitted no change. Yet they reduced what was excessive and augmented what was insufficient, simply adapting institutions to attain what was fitting for the time. Such were the means [?]: for example, simplicity was replaced by refinement, and the chou month by the zi month as the beginning of the year. Written records now survive in full; I have studied them and firmly follow them. Is there anything that cannot be known? By using the past to infer the future, even a hundred generations can consequently be known. Moreover, the Master, occupying a subordinate position, did not act contrary to his superiors; hence he said, “I follow the Zhou.” When it came to the abuses of Zhou practice, however, he wished to follow the men of earlier times and aspired to the finest practices of the Three Dynasties. Thus he expressed his concern with tireless earnestness. Alas, he possessed virtue but held no position! Nevertheless, these rites remain the same through ten thousand generations as through a single day. Great indeed was his achievement in transmitting instruction to posterity!

“Treat those from afar with kindness, and people from the four quarters will turn to you; cherish the feudal lords, and all under Heaven will stand in awe of you.”
Jiang Xin.

translation_en:
…This is how the meaning should be treated.
Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: Most who write on this topic quote extensively from the Questions and Answers (Huowen), stringing passages together into an essay. This is the only piece I have seen that is both clear and comprehensive.
Associate Examiner Qiu, Acting Bureau Director, comments: Refined and vigorous, concise and clear.
Examiner Peng, Right Mentor, comments: Orderly and polished.
Examiner Zhang, Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy, comments: There are no wasted words, yet the meaning is fully conveyed.
The Doctrine of the Mean says that measures of government extending to all under Heaven each have their corresponding effects. How difficult it is for government to reach all under Heaven! If distant peoples and the feudal lords have indeed been moved, could this happen without the requisite measures of government? In elucidating the Way’s pervasive operation and hidden subtlety, the Doctrine of the Mean quotes Confucius’s response to Duke Ai’s inquiry about government, reaching this point. It is as though he said: Can the effects of the nine guiding principles extend only from oneself to one’s family, and from the court to the state?
There are distant peoples in the world; our concern should simply be that we have not fully observed the proper way of treating them. If we truly know how to show them kindness, so that their coming and going meet no obstruction and they may freely choose whether to leave or remain, then many will receive our beneficence, and our transforming influence will reach far. Guests will feel at home upon arriving, and all will gladly serve as envoys to our state. Travelers will all be pleased and will certainly wish to take our roads. Who could prevent people from the four quarters from turning to us?
There are feudal lords; our concern should simply be that we have not fully observed the proper way of dealing with them. If we truly know how to cherish them, sharing their joys and sorrows and ensuring that their wealth and resources do not run short, then our virtue will be widely bestowed and our authority will hold broad sway. Cherishing our virtue, they will enjoy peace: those who serve as our fences, walls, screens, and bulwarks will all be loyal. Wherever government reaches, its effects respond in kind in this way. Should not those who possess the realm know what to devote themselves to? Yet Lu at that time could not win over Zhuanyu, close though it was, nor restrain the powerful Jisun clan. What sort of ruler was Duke Ai, that the Master should tell him these things? Ah! It was simply that he had not secured the right men. The restoration of the three estates [?] and the demolition of the three fortified cities were indeed results already demonstrated in practice. Why, then, was the aspiration to establish an Eastern Zhou never brought to completion?
Cheng Jian said to Duke Jing of Qi: “He is a man, and I am a man. Why should I fear him?” Yan Yuan said: “What sort of person was Shun? What sort of person am I? text:
大賢歷引古人自勵之言欲世子之信乎道也
夫性道之同聖賢固可及也觀諸古人之言豈
不益信矣乎孟子言滕世子之意如此且天下
無性外之道亦無不可盡性之人吾言性善而
道一者非無徵也不聞成覸之告景公乎聖賢
于我鈞丈夫也亦是性也豈在彼之有餘在我
之不足吾能自彊而彼可及矣尚何畏哉不聞
顏淵之自謂乎大舜與予猶夫人也亦是性也
彼爲法於天下可傳於後世人能有爲則亦若
===
是矣豈有異哉不惟是也公明儀不曰周公不
言文王我師斯言也盖有感于性善之同而自
切夫儀刑之念殆非以誣我也我固以爲然也
由是觀之則吾言亦足信而世子可力行矣行
之而有弗至者哉雖然世子可謂賢矣一聞善
言遂有志于古道而問禮問井地者相繼也其
弗克振者勢爾吁可慨夫
易
知至至之可與存義也

知終終之可與存義也
punctuated:
大賢歷引古人自勵之言，欲世子之信乎道也。夫性道之同，聖賢固可及也。觀諸古人之言，豈不益信矣乎？孟子言滕世子之意如此。且天下無性外之道，亦無不可盡性之人。吾言性善而道一者，非無徵也。不聞成覸之告景公乎？聖賢于我，鈞丈夫也，亦是性也，豈在彼之有餘，在我之不足？吾能自彊，而彼可及矣，尚何畏哉？不聞顏淵之自謂乎？大舜與予，猶夫人也，亦是性也。彼爲法於天下，可傳於後世，人能有爲，則亦若是矣，豈有異哉？不惟是也，公明儀不曰：「周公不言，文王我師。」斯言也，盖有感于性善之同，而自切夫儀刑之念，殆非以誣我也。我固以爲然也。由是觀之，則吾言亦足信，而世子可力行矣。行之而有弗至者哉？雖然，世子可謂賢矣。一聞善言，遂有志于古道，而問禮、問井地者相繼也。其弗克振者，勢爾。吁，可慨夫！

《易》
知至至之，可與存義也。
translation_en:
The great worthy cited in succession the words with which men of antiquity had encouraged themselves, wishing the heir apparent to have faith in the Way. Since human nature and the Way are shared by all, the sages and worthies can indeed be equaled. Considering the words of the ancients, would one not believe this still more firmly? Such was Mencius’s intention in speaking to the heir apparent of Teng.

Moreover, nowhere under Heaven is there a Way outside human nature, nor anyone incapable of fully realizing that nature. My assertion that human nature is good and the Way is one is not without evidence. Have you not heard what Cheng Jian told Duke Jing? “The sages and worthies are men just as I am, possessing this same nature. How could they have it in abundance while I lack it? If I exert myself, I can equal them. What, then, need I fear?” Have you not heard what Yan Yuan said of himself? “The great Shun and I are alike human beings, possessing this same nature. He became a model for all under Heaven, one that could be handed down to later generations. Anyone capable of purposeful action can likewise become such a person. What difference could there be?”

Nor is this all. Did Gongming Yi not say, “The Duke of Zhou did not speak; King Wen is my teacher” [?]? These words surely arose from his awareness that the goodness of human nature is shared by all, and from his own earnest desire to take the sages as models. They could hardly have been intended to deceive me. I certainly consider them true. Viewed in this light, my words too deserve belief, and the heir apparent can diligently put them into practice. If he practices them, could he fail to attain the goal?

Even so, the heir apparent may indeed be called worthy. Upon hearing good words just once, he set his heart on the ancient Way; his inquiries about ritual and the well-field system followed in succession. That he could not bring about a revival was due to circumstances alone. Alas, how lamentable!

Book of Changes

“Knowing the point to be reached and reaching it, one may thereby preserve righteousness.”

When one knows the ultimate reach of principle and exerts one’s strength to attain it, the operation of principle can be preserved. 理之會歸為吾之所當終也于是操持之定而
言必顧其行見於事者無不誠即其所真知而
施之素履知先而行實赴焉因其所心得而守
之終身志至而力必至焉夫如是而不可與存
義乎蓋自其理之致一者曰終自其一之散殊
者曰義不得其終則億見者無所定而變賾者
難於恒未可與存義也惟知終終之吾知誠則
自明而一以制天下之動安而能慮而簡以御
天下之煩雖時宜未措所以裁酌而協中者無
===

子歸之聖智之事而以為學之始終也吁後之

punctuated:
理之會歸為吾之所當終也，于是操持之定而言必顧其行，見於事者無不誠。即其所真知而施之素履，知先而行實赴焉；因其所心得而守之終身，志至而力必至焉。夫如是而不可與存義乎？蓋自其理之致一者曰終，自其一之散殊者曰義。不得其終，則億見者無所定，而變賾者難於恒，未可與存義也。惟知終終之，吾知誠則自明，而一以制天下之動；安而能慮，而簡以御天下之煩。雖時宜未措，所以裁酌而協中者無不具矣；雖事幾未來，所以權宜以濟變者無不備矣。君子之修業，其事如此，所以終日乾乾而夕猶惕若者，有由然哉！抑知至至之，知終終之，知行並進，聖學也。是即惟精惟一之傳、博文約禮之教也。然知行二而聖學晦也久矣。故程夫子歸之聖智之事，而以為學之始終也。吁！後之有志者，尚無忘於此致力歟！

通乎晝夜之道而知
潘滋
translation_en:
…the point at which principle converges is what I must carry through to completion. Thus, steadfast in maintaining it, one ensures that one’s words accord with one’s conduct, and everything manifested in affairs is sincere. One applies what one truly knows to one’s everyday conduct: knowledge leads, and action actually follows it. One holds throughout life to what one has grasped in the heart: wherever the resolve reaches, effort must reach as well. Acting thus, could one not preserve righteousness?

For the convergence of principle into unity is called its completion; the differentiation of that unity into its manifold particulars is called righteousness. Without grasping its completion, conjectural views [?] have nothing to settle upon, and amid intricate changes constancy is difficult to maintain; one cannot yet preserve righteousness. Only by knowing the point of completion and carrying it through does my understanding become clear through sincerity, so that unity governs all movement under Heaven. Being settled, one can deliberate, and simplicity thereby masters all the complexities under Heaven. Though the requirements of the moment have not yet presented themselves, everything needed to weigh and judge them in accordance with the mean is already present. Though the incipient developments of affairs have not yet arrived, everything needed to exercise discretion and respond successfully to change is already prepared.

Such is the superior man’s cultivation of his undertaking. There is good reason why he remains tirelessly active throughout the day and still watchful in the evening! Moreover, to know the point to be reached and reach it, and to know the point of completion and carry it through, is to advance knowledge and action together: this is the learning of the sages. It is precisely the transmitted teaching of being discerning and single-minded, and the instruction to broaden one’s learning in culture and restrain it through ritual. Yet knowledge and action have long been treated as separate, obscuring the learning of the sages. Hence Master Cheng assigned these to the work of sageliness and wisdom, regarding them as the beginning and end of learning. Ah! May those of later generations who possess the resolve never forget to devote their efforts to this!

“Comprehending the Way of Day and Night, He Knows”
By Pan Zi 潘滋.

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之奧彼知晝者疑于動矣然物而不化道滯於
動乎是知幽也死也鬼也晝矣而有夜動無動
也會一神於兩在蓋不惟知夫晝焉知夜者疑
于靜矣然往而不反道淪於靜乎是知明也生
也神也夜矣而有晝靜無靜也昭至微于至著
蓋不惟知夫夜焉寂感之至神一晝夜之推盪
道之所寓而存存不已者自與之渾融也顯微
之無間一晝夜之循環道之所在而生生不息
者自為之默契也夫謂之通知信乎命自我立
===
亦自我行範圍曲成皆由此出而非聞見之知
矣聖人用易至命一至是乎抑此言聖人至命
之事實則窮理盡性而至命非可以先後判也
其云用易以窮之盡之至之者見易道之大而
聖人盡之亦自夫人所同者極之焉耳矣卑之
者失之泛高之者失之虛其於易何吁玩孟子
脩身立命之說則於易也幾矣

平康正直彊弗友剛克燮友柔克沉潛剛

書

punctuated:
之奧。彼知晝者疑于動矣，然物而不化，道滯於動乎？是知幽也、死也、鬼也，晝矣而有夜，動無動也。會一神於兩在，蓋不惟知夫晝焉。知夜者疑于靜矣，然往而不反，道淪於靜乎？是知明也、生也、神也，夜矣而有晝，靜無靜也。昭至微于至著，蓋不惟知夫夜焉。寂感之至神，一晝夜之推盪，道之所寓，而存存不已者自與之渾融也；顯微之無間，一晝夜之循環，道之所在，而生生不息者自為之默契也。夫謂之通知，信乎命自我立，亦自我行，範圍曲成皆由此出，而非聞見之知矣。聖人用易至命，一至是乎？抑此言聖人至命之事，實則窮理盡性而至命，非可以先後判也。其云用易以窮之、盡之、至之者，見易道之大，而聖人盡之，亦自夫人所同者極之焉耳矣。卑之者失之泛，高之者失之虛，其於易何？吁！玩孟子脩身立命之說，則於易也幾矣。
書
平康正直，彊弗友剛克，燮友柔克，沉潛剛
translation_en:
…the profundities of yin and yang. Those who know day may be perplexed by activity. Yet if things remained fixed without transformation, would the Way be obstructed in activity? Thus one knows obscurity, death, and the spirits of the departed: within day there is night, and activity is without activity. One apprehends a single spiritual efficacy in its twofold presence; hence this is not merely knowing day. Those who know night may be perplexed by stillness. Yet if things went forth without returning, would the Way sink into stillness? Thus one knows brightness, life, and the spirits: within night there is day, and stillness is without stillness. One illuminates the most subtle within the most manifest; hence this is not merely knowing night.

The consummate spiritual efficacy of quiescence and response unifies the reciprocal motions of day and night. This is where the Way resides, and that which preserves itself unceasingly naturally merges with it. The absence of any interval between the manifest and the subtle unifies the cycle of day and night. This is where the Way is present, and that which generates life without cessation naturally accords with it in silence. What is called comprehensive understanding indeed means that Heaven’s mandate is established by oneself and also carried into effect by oneself. Encompassing all things and bringing each to fulfillment proceeds from this; it is not knowledge gained through hearing and seeing. Does the sage’s use of the Changes to attain an understanding of Heaven’s mandate truly reach such a height?

Yet although this speaks of the sage’s attainment of Heaven’s mandate, in fact fathoming principle, fully realizing one’s nature, and attaining Heaven’s mandate cannot be divided into successive stages. To speak of using the Changes to fathom, realize, and attain these things shows the greatness of the Way of the Changes. In fully realizing it, the sage merely takes what all people share and carries it to its utmost extent. Those who lower it err in making it superficial; those who exalt it err in making it empty. What understanding of the Changes do they have? Ah! Ponder Mencius’s teaching on cultivating oneself and establishing one’s destiny, and one will come close to understanding the Changes.

text:
過而為強戾弗順者必至于梗化其威以奪之
使之懼惡而不為有弱之過而為和柔委順者
必無以自立其福以予之使之慕善而勇為一
以剛克剛一以柔克柔隨其入而政以治之者
有二也亦有沉深潜退者狃于狹小而不及乎
中矣則激勵振拔進之於正大之體亦有高亢
明爽者鶩于虛遠而過乎中矣則丁寧告戒退
之於近易之歸一以剛克柔一以柔克剛隨其
入而教以化之者亦二也是則三德並持而施
===
之各當其可所措者約所制者廣聖人納天下
民俗于皇極有以哉嘗觀有虞之世可謂平康
矣而猶以不親命契猾夏命臯陶則正直剛柔
之為用其可缺一乎故立皇極以示其路達三
德以要其歸若八政之目皆其所顯設者也操
之有本施之有方化成天下周家有成效矣後
世徒把持以一切之法而三德亡噫王霸之辨
治忽之分其在兹歟
爾尚式時周公之猷訓惟日孜孜無敢逸

過而為強戾弗順者，必至于梗化，其威以奪之，使之懼惡而不為；有弱之過而為和柔委順者，必無以自立，其福以予之，使之慕善而勇為。一以剛克剛，一以柔克柔，隨其入而政以治之者有二也。亦有沉深潜退者，狃于狹小而不及乎中矣，則激勵振拔，進之於正大之體；亦有高亢明爽者，鶩于虛遠而過乎中矣，則丁寧告戒，退之於近易之歸。一以剛克柔，一以柔克剛，隨其入而教以化之者亦二也。是則三德並持，而施之各當其可，所措者約，所制者廣。聖人納天下民俗于皇極，有以哉！嘗觀有虞之世，可謂平康矣，而猶以不親命契，猾夏命臯陶，則正直剛柔之為用，其可缺一乎？故立皇極以示其路，達三德以要其歸，若八政之目，皆其所顯設者也。操之有本，施之有方，化成天下，周家有成效矣。後世徒把持以一切之法，而三德亡。噫！王霸之辨，治忽之分，其在兹歟？

translation_en:
…those whose excessive firmness makes them violent, recalcitrant, and unsubmissive will inevitably obstruct moral transformation. Use authority to subdue them, making them fear wrongdoing and refrain from it. Those whose excessive weakness makes them yielding, pliant, and compliant will have no means of standing on their own. Bestow blessings upon them, making them admire goodness and act upon it courageously. In one case, firmness masters firmness; in the other, gentleness masters gentleness. These are the two ways of governing them through administrative measures suited to their dispositions [?]. There are also those who are withdrawn, reserved, and retiring: habituated to narrowness, they fall short of the mean. Encourage and rouse them, advancing them toward an upright and expansive disposition. There are also those who are lofty, assertive, clear-minded, and spirited: pursuing the empty and remote, they exceed the mean. Admonish them earnestly, drawing them back toward what is accessible and easy to practice. In one case, firmness masters gentleness; in the other, gentleness masters firmness. These, too, are two ways of transforming them through instruction suited to their dispositions [?]. Thus the three virtues are maintained together, and each is applied as circumstances require: the measures employed are few, but their reach is broad. There is good reason why the sage brings the customs of the people throughout the realm into accord with the August Ultimate! Looking back at the age of Youyu, one may call it peaceful and tranquil. Yet Shun still charged Xie with addressing the lack of affection among people, and Gao Yao with dealing with those who disturbed the Chinese realm. Could any one of uprightness, firmness, and gentleness, then, be dispensed with in practice? Thus the August Ultimate is established to show people the way, and the three virtues are put into practice to bring them to their proper destination. Such matters as the eight branches of government are all its concrete institutional expressions. With a foundation for their direction and appropriate methods for their application, the Zhou house achieved proven results in transforming and perfecting the realm. Later generations merely sought to maintain control through indiscriminate laws, and the three virtues disappeared. Alas! Does not the distinction between kingly and hegemonic rule, and the division between order and disorder, lie here?

You should follow these plans and instructions of the Duke of Zhou, striving diligently every day, never daring to indulge in ease…

Jiang Xin 蔣信.

Comment by Associate Examiner Pan, Instructor: When King Cheng addressed Jun Chen, he wished him to move and transform the obstinate people of Yin. His words had a particular purpose, which this composition adequately brings out. It should be recorded as a model for those who indulge in empty rhetoric.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: In its exposition, the essay brings forward Jun Chen’s virtues of filial devotion and brotherly affection and urges him to further effort. The intent of the royal charge at that time appears vividly before our eyes.

Comment by Associate Examiner Qiu, Acting Bureau Director: It captures King Cheng’s original intent in charging Jun Chen.

Comment by Examiner Peng, Right Admonitor: He understands that the emphasis falls on the word “virtue.” This is indeed correct.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: Subtle and graceful, with lingering resonance.

When a worthy king encourages a great minister to follow instructions concerning illustrious virtue, he must also show him their efficacy. Virtue is the foundation of government. Moreover, when enduring instructions exist, how could one fail to know where to direct one’s efforts? Formerly, when King Cheng charged Jun Chen, his meaning was this: “The people of the eastern suburbs are the people whom the Duke of Zhou governed; the administration of the eastern suburbs is the administration that the Duke of Zhou conducted. Yet the means by which he moved and transformed them, and sustained them, rested solely upon virtue. How could you fail to take this as your model? You have heard that the fragrance of perfect government is ultimately attributable to illustrious virtue. Rooted in one’s own person and borne out among the people, it possesses a power that penetrates everywhere without obstruction. How supremely subtle it is! You [two illegible characters] …

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
尚由是訓而以愼德爲大要根諸心形諸事有
所以變化不測者寓何至微也爾其尚遵是訓
而以修德爲先務孝雖美行無以爲已至也惕
勵其志務求敬典在德而無一行之不美友雖
善事無以爲已能也懋勉其力務求克施有政
而無一事之未善位周公位也盍反之一于身厥
德有弗替于前人矣乎盖曰惟不足而祇勤之
不怠治周公治也盍驗之于己厥德有或斁于
往訓矣乎盖曰如不及而進修之不暇若遊于
===
逸則宴安之氣勝而德荒矣其無敢少自逸焉
可也若溺于豫則悅樂之情恣而德塞矣其無
敢少自豫焉可也逸豫不生而功力不隳德于
是明矣推之爲政則君陳亦周公也其於至治
也何有嗟夫殷民爲梗相繼而治之者以周公
以君陳又終之以畢公世變風移式化厥訓有
周深仁厚澤之施於此可想見矣然先後元勳
也君陳獨中處而與之並雖不得與十人之列
猶及同事於二公之間嗚呼賢哉

punctuated: 尚由是訓，而以愼德爲大要。根諸心，形諸事，有所以變化不測者寓，何至微也！爾其尚遵是訓，而以修德爲先務。孝雖美行，無以爲已至也；惕勵其志，務求敬典在德，而無一行之不美。友雖善事，無以爲已能也；懋勉其力，務求克施有政，而無一事之未善。位，周公位也，盍反之一于身：厥德有弗替于前人矣乎？盖曰惟不足，而祇勤之不怠。治，周公治也，盍驗之于己：厥德有或斁于往訓矣乎？盖曰如不及，而進修之不暇。若遊于逸，則宴安之氣勝而德荒矣，其無敢少自逸焉可也。若溺于豫，則悅樂之情恣而德塞矣，其無敢少自豫焉可也。逸豫不生，而功力不隳，德于是明矣。推之爲政，則君陳亦周公也，其於至治也何有！嗟夫！殷民爲梗，相繼而治之者，以周公，以君陳，又終之以畢公。世變風移，式化厥訓，有周深仁厚澤之施，於此可想見矣。然先後元勳也，君陳獨中處而與之並，雖不得與十人之列，猶及同事於二公之間。嗚呼，賢哉！
translation_en:
…follow this instruction, and make watchfulness over virtue your chief concern. Rooted in the heart and manifested in affairs, it contains the means of effecting transformations beyond measure. How utterly subtle it is! You should follow this instruction and make the cultivation of virtue your first duty. Though filial devotion is admirable conduct, do not suppose that you have already attained perfection. Keep your resolve vigilant and vigorous; strive to honor the enduring norms through virtue, so that none of your conduct falls short of excellence. Though brotherly affection is a good thing, do not suppose that you have already mastered it. Exert yourself diligently; strive to extend it into government, so that nothing you do falls short of goodness. Your position is the position held by the Duke of Zhou. Why not turn your scrutiny wholly upon yourself and ask: does your virtue uphold the example of your predecessor without decline? The point is to remain conscious of your insufficiency and diligently apply yourself without flagging. Your government is the government of the Duke of Zhou. Why not examine yourself and ask: has your virtue in any way fallen away from the instructions of the past? The point is to advance in self-cultivation as though you could never catch up, with no time to spare. If you wander into indolence, the disposition toward ease and comfort will prevail, and virtue will fall into neglect. You must therefore never dare indulge yourself in the slightest idleness. If you become immersed in pleasure, your desire for enjoyment will run unchecked, and virtue will be obstructed. You must therefore never dare indulge yourself in the slightest pleasure. When indolence and pleasure do not arise, and sustained effort does not slacken, virtue will thereby become bright. Extend this into government, and Jun Chen too will be a Duke of Zhou. What difficulty will there then be in attaining perfect government?

Alas! The people of Yin were recalcitrant. Those who governed them in succession were the Duke of Zhou, Jun Chen, and finally the Duke of Bi. As the generations changed and customs shifted, the people were transformed by following their instructions. Here one can envision the profound benevolence and abundant beneficence bestowed by the Zhou dynasty. Yet those who came before and after were both founding statesmen of outstanding merit. Jun Chen alone stood between them and ranked alongside them. Though he did not gain a place among the ten worthy ministers, he nevertheless came to serve between these two dukes. Ah, how worthy he was!

而知愛咸欲作之君以蒙其休是雖鎬京之未

之師以率其敎是雖辟雍之未啓而先已思服

translation_en:
…[?]. Speaking of the poem Xia Wu (Successors to the Martial Kings), it praises King Wu for succeeding the three kings and possessing all under Heaven. Its meaning is that our King Wu’s filial piety had already become a model for all under Heaven. The people of the world revered him and knew to love him; all wished him to be their ruler so that they might receive his blessings. Thus, even before he had established his residence at Haojing, they had already united around him. Observing and taking him as their model, they trusted him and then followed him; all wished him to be their teacher so that they might follow his instruction. Thus, even before the Biyong royal academy had opened, they already wished to submit to him. That a moving influence should evoke a response is inherent in principle. How much more so when establishing love through affection for one’s parents awakens the excellence of the constant moral nature people possess! Those sharing his virtue were therefore by no means limited to ten men. That responding should lead to affection is inherent in human feeling. How much more so when guiding people through virtue awakens their innate moral understanding! Those drawn to him were therefore by no means limited to the men and women of the eastern expedition. Could King Wu have seized this for himself? It was simply that he never forgot his filial thoughts: his mind constantly dwelt upon his ancestors’ ascending and descending spirits, seeking to continue the virtue transmitted through the generations and to accord with Heaven’s Mandate. Thus his heart was pure. Reverent morning and night, his sincerity uninterrupted from beginning to end, he fulfilled the trust befitting a king and became a model for those below and above. Thus his filial piety endured.

From King Tai to Wang Ji and then to King Wen, the foundations of kingship gradually emerged from obscurity into prominence. When King Wu succeeded them, the people’s hearts united and the state’s standing rose: was this not still greater prominence? From laying the foundations, to laboring for the ruling house, to bringing peace to the Xia lands, Heaven’s Mandate gradually emerged from obscurity into clarity. When King Wu succeeded them, the royal enterprise was accomplished and all under Heaven became one: was this not its brilliant manifestation? Thus the common people bore witness to their trust and allegiance, while his continuation of his ancestors’ undertakings shed glory upon their earlier achievements. There is good reason to call King Wu’s filial piety all-embracing! Yet vast indeed is the Way of filial piety. In the three kings it is called virtue, and therefore he sought it; in Heaven it is called the Mandate…

於赫湯孫穆穆厥聲庸鼓有斁萬舞有
奕我有嘉客亦不夷懌

是以配也；在武謂之孚，是以成也。合而言之，孝也。求德者，孝之積也；配命者，孝之純也；成孚者，孝之實也。合而言之，敬也。敬，其孝之聚乎？
鞉鼓淵淵，嘒嘒管聲。旣和且平，依我磬聲。於赫湯孫，穆穆厥聲。庸鼓有斁，萬舞有奕。我有嘉客，亦不夷懌？

translation_en:
…and thus it is matched. In King Wu it is called trust, and thus it is brought to fulfillment. Taken together, these constitute filial piety. Seeking virtue is the accumulation of filial piety; matching Heaven’s mandate is the purity of filial piety; bringing trust to fulfillment is the substantial realization of filial piety. Taken together, these constitute reverence. Is reverence not the gathering together of filial piety?
The hand drums and great drums resound deeply;
clear and shrill are the sounds of the pipes.
Harmonious and balanced,
they follow the sound of our stone chimes.
How illustrious is Tang’s descendant!
How solemn is his music!
The great bells and drums sound in abundance;
the wan dance is splendid.
We have excellent guests:
are they not at ease and delighted?
Tang Shunzhi
Associate Examiner Su, Assistant Instructor, comments: “Candidates generally can discuss the performance of the music from beginning to end. When they reach the final four lines, however, most fail to give them a proper place in their argument. They do not understand that the opening speaks of ‘presenting the offering and approaching the spirits, thinking of fulfillment’; here it finally praises the beauty of that achievement. This must not be passed over. This composition grasps the point, and therefore I have selected it for inclusion.”
Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: “The earlier and later passages discussing music are very difficult to arrange neatly. Yet this candidate alone can recount the proceedings and shape them into a coherent composition. Its rhythms are distinctly audible; reading it makes one forget fatigue.”
Associate Examiner Cao, Instructor, comments: “The narration and argument are meticulous and closely woven; the sounds and cadences are harmonious and balanced. Does it not have the lingering resonance of one voice singing and three voices responding?”
Associate Examiner Wang, Secretary, comments: “The composition is also orderly in its structure.”
Examiner Peng, Right Mentor, comments: “It fully conveys every nuance of the Shang people’s intention in enumerating these excellences.”
Examiner Zhang, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Reading his composition is like hearing the music itself.”

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
商人之祀先樂盛而歸之主祭者樂成而感乎
助祭者甚矣商之重祭也作樂之美至于感神
人而孝敬之道昭矣此盖祀成湯之樂至此意
謂我商以思成爲孝而作樂以尚聲爲恭方其
三闋正稀廣牡初薦而始作之也八音備矣小
而鞉鼓其亦淵淵乎衆樂陳矣微而管籥其亦
嘒嘒乎作于堂下而有旣和且平之休其相濟
如五味也協之堂上而有依我磬聲之美其有
序如四時也主是祭者伊誰乎於赫哉此湯孫
===
===
也而制禮作樂之得其情穆穆哉此樂聲也而
美德告功之有其具所謂思成之賚而有不在
是哉殆夫十倫旣備九獻以畢而其成終也洪
鐘旣宣而條理爲之不濫楹鼓交作而音節爲
之常明奏以文也則飾以羽旄而有綴兆舒疾
之度亂以武也則動以干戚而有發揚蹈厲之
風助是祭者何如乎盖雖先代之後作賓于王
而皆以聞樂爲喜矣在位之士讓德于廟而忘
其異代之悲矣況於烈祖之神而顧不我格哉

punctuated: 商人之祀先，樂盛而歸之主祭者，樂成而感乎助祭者。甚矣，商之重祭也！作樂之美至于感神人，而孝敬之道昭矣。此盖祀成湯之樂。至此，意謂我商以思成爲孝，而作樂以尚聲爲恭。方其三闋正稀，廣牡初薦，而始作之也，八音備矣，小而鞉鼓，其亦淵淵乎；衆樂陳矣，微而管籥，其亦嘒嘒乎。作于堂下，而有旣和且平之休，其相濟如五味也；協之堂上，而有依我磬聲之美，其有序如四時也。主是祭者伊誰乎？於赫哉，此湯孫也，而制禮作樂之得其情；穆穆哉，此樂聲也，而美德告功之有其具。所謂思成之賚，而有不在是哉？殆夫十倫旣備，九獻以畢，而其成終也，洪鐘旣宣，而條理爲之不濫；楹鼓交作，而音節爲之常明。奏以文也，則飾以羽旄，而有綴兆舒疾之度；亂以武也，則動以干戚，而有發揚蹈厲之風。助是祭者何如乎？盖雖先代之後，作賓于王，而皆以聞樂爲喜矣；在位之士，讓德于廟，而忘其異代之悲矣。況於烈祖之神，而顧不我格哉？
translation_en:
When the people of Shang sacrificed to their ancestors, the magnificence of the music was attributed to the principal sacrificant, and its completion moved those assisting at the sacrifice. How greatly Shang esteemed sacrifice! The beauty of its music reached the point of moving spirits and human beings alike, making manifest the way of filial devotion and reverence. This was presumably the music for sacrificing to Cheng Tang. At this point, the meaning is that we of Shang take remembrance that brings the ancestors’ presence to realization as filial devotion, and, in making music, esteem sound as an expression of reverence.

When the three musical movements were “properly sparse” [?], the great bull was first presented and the music began. All eight classes of instruments were present: even the small pellet drum sounded deep and resonant. The full ensemble was arrayed: even the slender pipes and flutes sounded clear and bright. Played below the hall, the music possessed the excellence of being both harmonious and balanced, its sounds complementing one another like the five flavors. Coordinated with the music above the hall, it possessed the beauty of “following the sound of our chime stones,” its order resembling that of the four seasons. Who presided over this sacrifice? How illustrious—this descendant of Tang, who grasped the true spirit of instituting ritual and making music! How solemn—these musical sounds, fully equipped to praise virtue and proclaim achievement! Could any of the blessings said to come from remembrance that realizes the ancestors’ presence be absent here?

When the ten relationships expressed in music were fully embodied and the nine libations completed, the performance reached its conclusion. The great bells rang out, yet the ordered arrangement of the music did not become excessive; the pillar drums sounded in alternation, and its rhythm remained clear throughout. In the civil dance, the dancers were adorned with feathers and yak-tail plumes, observing prescribed measures for their positions, the bounds of the dancing ground, and the slowness or speed of their movements. In the concluding martial dance, they moved with shields and battle-axes, displaying the vigor of rising, stamping, and forceful movement.

What of those assisting at this sacrifice? Even the descendants of former dynasties, serving as guests of the king, all rejoiced to hear the music. The men holding office deferred to virtue in the ancestral temple and forgot their sorrow at living under a different dynasty. How much more, then, would the spirit of the illustrious ancestor come to us!

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄

人也故諱之也

translation_en:
…Thus, with everything complete from beginning to end, spirits and men alike rejoiced: the music of Shang may indeed be called consummate music. Without sincerity and filial devotion, how could one attain this? Moreover, the Record of Rites says: “When ritual and music are manifest and complete, Heaven and Earth perform their offices.” In the ode Na, drums accompany the reception of the sacrificial victim; the hand drum, pipes, and chime stones mark the opening of the sacrifice; and the great bells, drums, and the wan dance mark its completion. Could each individual act constitute a complete musical movement in itself? Yet, savoring its words, one finds that its passages seem to illuminate one another, leaving lingering resonances. This is why the Hymns of Shang are spare and archaic, and why Zengzi sang them. Nevertheless, the Huo music was indeed martial. Jizha said: “Such is the sage’s greatness, and yet there remains something shameful in his virtue.” The Master discussed the Shao and Wu music but did not mention this: he was a descendant of Yin, and therefore passed over it out of deference.

切文宇謹嚴可以為明經者式矣

分地委于內春秋貶惡之意深分地易于外春

盖宣王以母弟懿親賜之方嶽以備時巡之朝
者然他國未有是也鄭宜何如其世守邪莊也

之畿內以供入覲之需者然他國未有是也魯

When an allotted territory was handed over to our state, the Spring and Autumn Annals conveyed a profound intention to condemn wrongdoing; when an allotted territory was exchanged away to another state, the Annals conveyed a profound intention to veil wrongdoing. In this exchange of Beng and Xu, Zheng and Lu were equally culpable. How fitting that the Annals should convey its judgment of each through its manner of recording the events!
What was Beng? It was Zheng’s estate for bathing and purification. King Xuan, because the recipient was his beloved younger brother born of the same mother, granted him this estate near the regional sacred mountain to provide for attendance at court when the king made his periodic tours. Other states had no such estate. What ought Zheng to have done? Surely it should have preserved it through successive generations! Duke Zhuang considered Beng to be of no further use, and also saw an advantage in the proximity of Lu’s territory at Xu. Moreover, to resist Zifeng, was he not then seeking to secure Lu as an ally? Earlier, when proposing peaceful relations, he had verbally requested the exchange but had not yet handed over the land. Now Wan was specially dispatched as envoy, and Lu had already taken the territory into its registers. Evidently, Zheng considered that the Son of Heaven’s inspection tours would never again take place and that the territory allotted to its forebears need not be valued. Its lack of regard for ruler and kin was thus revealed. What wrongdoing in the world could be greater than this?
Furthermore, Lu was induced to disregard righteousness and covet what did not belong to it. Was this not because Zheng requested release from its duties concerning Mount Tai and invoked the sacrifices to the Duke of Zhou as a pretext? It is as though the Sage were saying: “To transfer Beng was Zheng’s intention; it would have been possible simply to record it.” Yet he wrote only, “We entered,” showing that the land did not originally belong to us, and that to force through what righteousness forbade was to act contrary to proper order. Such was his intention in condemning Zheng.
What was Xu? It was Lu’s lodging territory for attendance at the royal court. King Cheng, in recognition of the Duke of Zhou’s great achievements, granted it within the royal domain to provide for the needs of court audiences. Other states had no such territory. Lu…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
宜何如其世守邪桓也謂若無所事許而且利
鄭祊之償况子羽之難亦欲結之爲援乎先世
歸祊雖納其地未與易也至是鄭璧甫加魯田
遽授盖廢朝覲之禮棄先祖之地而無君親之
心亦見矣天下之惡孰大于是然使魯明于義
利過而知改豈不可請于王畿而復周公之宇
乎聖人若曰易許國惡也直錄不可也故諱易
言假若暫從彼請義可得而復之以自新者所
以諱魯之意如此是則一書法隱顯之間而君
===
親之重義利之防内外之辯咸寓矣抑莊桓之
惡不特是耳繻葛鍾巫之禍可勝誅哉然忽儀
亹突彭生之報亦宜矣因是而讀緇衣之詩周
禮之書固深慨二君之愧于先德也
晉伐鮮虞昭公十二年吳伐我哀公八年
康載

文但求詞義簡嚴曲盡斷制如此作者亦少錄
之可以祛牽合强比之譏矣

宜何如其世守邪？桓也謂若無所事許，而且利鄭祊之償，况子羽之難，亦欲結之爲援乎？先世歸祊，雖納其地，未與易也。至是鄭璧甫加，魯田遽授，盖廢朝覲之禮，棄先祖之地，而無君親之心亦見矣。天下之惡孰大于是？然使魯明于義利，過而知改，豈不可請于王畿，而復周公之宇乎？聖人若曰：「易許，國惡也，直錄不可也。」故諱易言假，若暫從彼請，義可得而復之以自新者，所以諱魯之意如此。是則一書法隱顯之間，而君親之重、義利之防、内外之辯咸寓矣。抑莊桓之惡不特是耳，繻葛、鍾巫之禍，可勝誅哉？然忽、儀、亹、突、彭生之報亦宜矣。因是而讀《緇衣》之詩、《周禮》之書，固深慨二君之愧于先德也。
晉伐鮮虞，昭公十二年。吳伐我，哀公八年。
康載。

translation_en:
…How ought Lu to have preserved it through the generations? Duke Huan thought that he had no use for Xu and coveted Zheng’s offer of Beng in exchange. Moreover, amid the troubles involving Ziyu [?], did he also wish to secure Zheng as an ally? When Beng had been transferred in the preceding reign, Lu had accepted the territory but had not agreed to an exchange. Now, scarcely had Zheng presented its jade disk before Lu’s land was handed over. Thus Lu abandoned the rites of attendance at the royal court and cast away its ancestors’ land, revealing its lack of regard for ruler and forebears. What evil in the world could be greater? Yet had Lu understood righteousness and profit, and recognized and corrected its error, could it not have petitioned the royal court and recovered the Duke of Zhou’s domain? It is as though the Sage said: “The exchange of Xu was a disgrace to our state; it cannot be recorded directly.” He therefore avoided “exchange” and wrote “lend,” as though Lu had only temporarily acceded to Zheng’s request and could rightfully recover the land and reform itself. Such was his intention in concealing Lu’s disgrace. Thus, within the concealment and disclosure of a single manner of recording, there reside the importance of ruler and forebears, the boundary between righteousness and profit, and the distinction between one’s own state and other states. Yet the evils of Dukes Zhuang and Huan were not confined to this. Could the disasters at Xuge and Zhongwu ever be condemned enough? The retribution involving Hu, Yi, Wei, Tu, and Pengsheng was therefore fitting. Reading the poem “Black Robes” and the Rites of Zhou in this light, one deeply laments how these two rulers fell shamefully short of their ancestors’ virtue.
“Jin attacked Xianyu”—the twelfth year of Duke Zhao. “Wu attacked us”—the eighth year of Duke Ai.
Kang Zai.
Comment by Associate Examiner Qian, School Instructor: The meaning of the commentary is clear and orderly, and seems easy to turn into an essay. Yet writers who achieve such concision and rigor in wording and meaning, while fully expressing its judgments in all their nuances, are few. Recording this essay can dispel criticism of strained connections and forced comparisons.

Associate Examiner Qin, a Bureau Secretary, comments: Candidates generally know that this topic should be argued in terms of trustworthiness and righteousness, and ritual propriety and righteousness. Yet exceedingly few can weave together the meaning of the commentary into an essay like this one. It therefore deserves inclusion.
Examiner Peng, Right Admonisher, comments: The language and reasoning are precise and rigorous.
Examiner Zhang, a Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting, comments: By analyzing the events on their own evidence, the interpretive principles become apparent of themselves.
The Spring and Autumn Annals sometimes severely condemns the wrongdoing of hegemons to illuminate trustworthiness and righteousness; sometimes it carefully conceals a state's humiliation to illuminate ritual propriety and righteousness. Here, Jin's attack on Xianyu was a failure in the use of arms, while Lu's covenant with the army of Wu was a failure in planning for the state. Examining the principles governing these entries, we find profound instruction from the Sage!
How deplorable that Jin, harboring ambitions to expand its territory and preparing to take military action against Xianyu, devised a scheme to borrow passage through another territory, resulting in its entry into Xiyang. The Spring and Autumn Annals does not give the ruler's rank or title, but records only the state's name: it treats Jin as barbarian. Now, when Duke Xian of Jin destroyed Yu, the designations “army” and “men” were used. The deceit was the same in both cases. Is treating Jin as barbarian not excessive? What makes the central states worthy of esteem is simply trustworthiness and righteousness. Once these are lost, what distinction remains between them and the alien peoples, the Yi and Di?
Qian of Chu destroyed Chen under the pretext of supporting Sun Wu; shortly afterward he destroyed Cai as well, having lured Ban of Cai into a trap. Relying on force and practicing deceit, he abandoned both trustworthiness and righteousness: this was, indeed, typical of barbarian nature. But what offense had Xianyu committed that Jin should wish to adopt the schemes of Jing-Chu? Alas! A hegemon is charged with repelling the barbarians. With Chu's aggression reaching such extremes, Jin could neither check it nor refrain from imitating it. How, then, was Jin any better than Chu? text:
狄之示人必以信義爲貴不可變詐如晉以致
傾危成俗而不可救爾若魯以入邾嘗挑釁于
強吳也乃因東陽之克而有萊門之盟春秋不
言四鄙及與吳盟諱之也夫三國戰郎直書來
戰此其受禍均爾諱之一何深乎盖所恃以立
國者禮義而已失之則與棄國無人奚異焉彼
國斃不從宋華元也背城借一齊國佐也執詞
從敵禮義自重皆謀國之良者今國勢未偪而
魯遽爲城下之盟乎魯國卿謀國者也吳釁至
===
此既不能敵而且辱焉猶謂國有人哉故略而
書伐所謂内以諱爲貶示人必以禮義自強不
可偷懦如魯以至侵削陵遲而莫之恥爾吁晉
以世伯至於效夷魯以人望至於辱國聖人至
是亦有甚弗獲已者矣嘗考季孫專魯故微虎
景伯冉有之忠及踊幕庭者七百人類擯不用
固也獨惜叔向知楚不信天將斃之苟吳他日
不受鼓人之叛乃亦至是何歟豈晉昭之弗信
用乎雖然晉魯自是日微矣君臣用舍可不慎
