punctuated: 狄之，示人必以信義爲貴，不可變詐如晉，以致傾危成俗而不可救爾。若魯以入邾，嘗挑釁于強吳也，乃因東陽之克而有萊門之盟。《春秋》不言四鄙及與吳盟，諱之也。夫三國戰郎，直書來戰，此其受禍均爾，諱之一何深乎？盖所恃以立國者禮義而已，失之則與棄國無人奚異焉？彼「國斃不從」，宋華元也；「背城借一」，齊國佐也。執詞從敵，禮義自重，皆謀國之良者。今國勢未偪，而魯遽爲城下之盟乎？魯國卿，謀國者也。吳釁至此，既不能敵而且辱焉，猶謂國有人哉？故略而書伐，所謂内以諱爲貶，示人必以禮義自強，不可偷懦如魯，以至侵削陵遲而莫之恥爾。吁！晉以世伯至於效夷，魯以人望至於辱國，聖人至是亦有甚弗獲已者矣。嘗考季孫專魯，故微虎、景伯、冉有之忠，及踊幕庭者七百人，類擯不用，固也。獨惜叔向知楚不信，天將斃之，苟吳他日不受鼓人之叛，乃亦至是，何歟？豈晉昭之弗信用乎？雖然，晉魯自是日微矣，君臣用舍可不慎
translation_en:
…treats them as barbarians, showing people that trustworthiness and righteousness must be prized. They must not practice deception and fraud as Jin did, allowing treachery to become customary beyond remedy. As for Lu, by invading Zhu it had provoked the powerful state of Wu; then, following the capture of Dongyang, it concluded the covenant at Laimen. The Spring and Autumn Annals mentions neither the four border regions nor the covenant with Wu, concealing these matters out of shame. Yet when the three states fought at Lang, it recorded straightforwardly that they “came to fight.” The calamities suffered were alike: why conceal this one so thoroughly? Ritual propriety and righteousness alone sustain a state. Once these are lost, how does it differ from a state abandoned, with no worthy men remaining? “Though the state perish, we shall not comply”: this was Hua Yuan of Song. “With our backs to the city wall, let us stake everything on one battle”: this was Guo Zuo of Qi. Upholding their declared terms in dealing with the enemy, and maintaining their dignity through ritual propriety and righteousness, both were worthy counselors of their states. Now Lu’s circumstances were not yet desperate, yet it hastened to conclude a covenant beneath its city walls! Lu’s ministers were responsible for planning on the state’s behalf. With Wu’s aggression reaching this point, they could neither resist it nor avoid humiliation. Could one still say that the state had worthy men? Thus the Annals omits the details and records an attack. This is what is meant by censuring one’s own state through concealment: it shows people that they must strengthen themselves through ritual propriety and righteousness. They must not be lax and cowardly like Lu, suffering encroachment, loss of territory, and decline without feeling shame.

Alas! Jin, whose rulers had been hegemons for generations, came to imitate the barbarians; Lu, upon which people had placed their hopes, came to disgrace its state. At this point the Sage, too, had compelling reasons for writing as he did. I have examined how the Jisun clan monopolized power in Lu. Thus it was only to be expected that loyal men such as Wei Hu, Jingbo, and Ran You, together with the seven hundred men who leaped in the tented courtyard [?], were generally excluded from service. One particularly regrets that, although Shu Xiang knew Chu was untrustworthy and that Heaven would destroy it, and Gou Wu [?] on another occasion refused to accept the rebellion of the people of Gu, matters nevertheless reached this point. Why was this? Was it because Duke Zhao of Jin failed to trust and employ them? Be that as it may, Jin and Lu grew weaker daily from this time onward. Can rulers and ministers afford to be careless in whom they employ or set aside…

即樂音之無患，而民之良心見矣。夫慈愛者，民之良心也。以其音之和柔而無患者見之，則樂非人心之所由生乎？記樂記者謂夫人心之微，而可以樂觀，豈惟哀樂敬怒為然哉？雖愛猶是
translation_en:
…indeed!

Book of Rites

“When sounds that are broad and ample, full and clear, smoothly formed and harmoniously moving arise, the people become compassionate and loving.”

Cheng Lie

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, School Instructor: Everyone knows and can say that sound arises from the human heart. But when it comes to describing sounds that are broad and ample, full and clear, smoothly formed and harmoniously moving, it is difficult to achieve a precise and fitting account. This essay alone excels among the submissions; hence its inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Left Judicial Reviewer: Of the six kinds of sound that arise, this alone is perfectly beautiful, because the feeling that produces it is good. Writers generally fail to examine this closely. Moreover, their explanations of compassion and love mostly consist of padding and stale verbiage, scarcely bearing on the subject. This essay alone grasps the meaning deeply, while its language is elegant and ample. Its concluding point is especially clear and readily understood. Its author is evidently deeply versed in classical learning.

Comment by Examiner Peng, Right Mentor: The explanation of compassion and love is good.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Expositor-in-waiting: It seems to grasp the subtlety of sound as the expression of the heart.

Precisely in the absence of distress in musical sounds, the people’s innate goodness becomes apparent. Compassion and love are the innate goodness of the people’s hearts. If this is revealed through the gentleness and freedom from distress of their sounds, does not music arise from the human heart? The writer of the Record of Music says that the subtle workings of the human heart can be observed through music. Can this be true only of sorrow, joy, reverence, and anger? Even love is likewise…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也故嘗求諸其音矣寬而不迫裕而有容音之
從容條暢有以盡其餘何志微噍殺之有肉爲
璧地好爲璧孔音之圓瑩通滑焉能得其妙何
繁文簡節之有至于粗厲猛賁不可謂順今其
成也小大既律終始既比所謂無相奪倫也非
順乎廉直勁正近于未和今其動也倡和有應
清濁有經所謂八音克諧也非和乎夫如是故
心之慈愛可得而觀矣誠以其中心慈者其聲
必寬裕肉好則可謂德音也故於堂下之聲者
===
固皆其心聲也其愛心感者其聲和順成和動
則可謂和矣藹然于搏拊之間者固皆其德音
也情見而義立非但其聲足樂也蓋雖愉色婉
容如將見之憂思康樂云乎哉樂終而德尊非
但其文足論也蓋雖下氣怡聲若或聞焉剛毅
肅敬云乎哉是則樂本于人心而可以觀德如
此謂樂不可以爲僞者詎不信然抑論凡民之
善慈愛爲本是謂不忍之心仁之發也故哀而
非此則傷于怨怒而非此則近於暴以敬行此

===

但其文足論也蓋雖下氣怡聲者或聞焉剛毅

此謂樂不可以爲僞者詎不信然抑論凡民之
音慈愛爲本是謂不忍之心仁之發也故哀而
非此則傷于怨怒而非此則近於暴以撒行此
punctuated: 也。故嘗求諸其音矣：寬而不迫，裕而有容，音之從容條暢，有以盡其餘，何志微噍殺之有？肉爲璧地，好爲璧孔，音之圓瑩通滑，焉能得其妙，何繁文簡節之有？至于粗厲猛賁，不可謂順。今其成也，小大既律，終始既比，所謂無相奪倫也，非順乎？廉直勁正，近于未和。今其動也，倡和有應，清濁有經，所謂八音克諧也，非和乎？夫如是，故心之慈愛可得而觀矣。誠以其中心慈者，其聲必寬裕肉好，則可謂德音也。故於堂下之聲者，固皆其心聲也。其愛心感者，其聲和順成和動，則可謂和矣。藹然于搏拊之間者，固皆其德音也。情見而義立，非但其聲足樂也。蓋雖愉色婉容，如將見之，憂思康樂云乎哉？樂終而德尊，非但其文足論也。蓋雖下氣怡聲，若或聞焉，剛毅肅敬云乎哉？是則樂本于人心，而可以觀德如此。謂樂不可以爲僞者，詎不信然？抑論凡民之善，慈愛爲本，是謂不忍之心，仁之發也。故哀而非此，則傷于怨；怒而非此，則近於暴；以敬行此
translation_en:
…is so as well. Thus I have sought it in the music’s tones. Broad without being constrained, ample and accommodating, the tones unfold unhurriedly and freely, fully expressing their abundance. How could there be any faintness or shrill attenuation [?]? The solid body is the substance of a jade disc; the opening is its central hole. In the tones’ rounded clarity and smooth fluency, how can their subtle excellence be attained [?], and how could there be elaborate ornament with sparse rhythm? As for roughness, harshness, and fierce impetuosity, these cannot be called concordant. Yet when the music reaches completion, its greater and lesser tones accord with the pitch standards, and its ending and beginning fit together. This is what is meant by none encroaching upon another’s proper order. Is this not concord? Sharpness, directness, force, and rectitude verge on a lack of harmony. Yet when the music is set in motion, the leading and answering voices respond to one another, and the high and low pitches follow their proper rules. This is what is meant by the eight classes of instruments achieving harmony. Is this not harmony?

Because it is thus, the heart’s kindness and love can be discerned. Truly, when a person is kind within, the sound must be broad and ample, with substance and openness, and may therefore be called the sound of virtue. Thus the sounds below the hall [?] are all the voice of that person’s heart. When a loving heart is stirred, its sound is harmonious and concordant, becoming harmonious and moving [?]; it may therefore be called harmony. The warmth manifest amid the beating and tapping of instruments is all the sound of that person’s virtue.

Feeling becomes manifest and rightness is established: it is not merely that the sound affords pleasure. Indeed, a cheerful countenance and gentle demeanor seem about to appear before one’s eyes. Can this be spoken of merely in terms of sorrowful reflection or peaceful enjoyment? The music ends and virtue is honored: it is not merely that its patterned form merits discussion. Indeed, a restrained breath and a pleasant voice seem almost audible. Can this be spoken of merely in terms of firmness, resolve, solemnity, and reverence? Thus music is rooted in the human heart, and in this way virtue can be discerned through it. Is the saying that music cannot be falsified not indeed true?

Moreover, speaking of goodness among the common people, kindness and love are its foundation. This is what is called the heart that cannot bear others’ suffering, the expression of benevolence. Thus grief without this is marred by resentment; anger without this approaches violence; to put this into practice with reverence…

translation_en:
…[Four illegible characters]. To take pleasure in licentious disorder is simply to lack an understanding of benevolence. Thus one cannot delight in music and also avoid licentiousness [?]. Otherwise, why would it be said: “If a person lacks benevolence, what can he do with music?”

“Filial piety, when established, fills Heaven and Earth; when extended, reaches across the Four Seas; when transmitted to later generations, admits of no distinction between morning and evening.”
Cheng Lie

Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: “Of the topics in ‘The Meaning of Sacrifices,’ this is the most difficult to develop fully. For vigorous expression and refined reasoning, no composition surpasses this one.”
Associate Examiner Jiang, Left Case Reviewer, comments: “This concerns the great source of filial piety. If an essay confines itself to the ordinary practices of serving one’s parents, I do not know how it could exhaust the subject. This piece is recorded to instruct those who study without attending to the root.”
Examiner Peng, Right Mentor, comments: “The reasoning is clear and the expression fluent.”
Examiner Zhang, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Here is someone who discusses filial piety well.”

The great worthy expounded the Way of filial piety as supremely flourishing and inexhaustible. Filial piety is the root of virtue. That it fills all space, spreads everywhere, and remains the same for later generations—is this not inherent in the essential nature of its Way? Master Zeng meant that, among all the ways under Heaven, none stands above filial piety; speaking of its utmost reach, nothing is excluded. How do I know this? Heaven and Earth occupy their appointed positions, the extremes of height and depth. What can stand alongside them and form a triad with them? It is filial piety…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也盖即其生物之德而流行以爲命凡所以敦
化顯仁盈兩間者皆是也所謂發育萬物峻極
于天直而立之不有以塞于天地乎四海一隅
廣遠之極也孰能散而周之乎是孝也盖即其
太和之運而保合以有生凡所爲慈愛惻怛者
舉天下皆然也所謂天下雷行物與無妄敷而
散之不有以横于四海乎然事有久而或弊故
勢有泥而不行皆小道爾今也屹然貞觀之道
歷萬世而無弊盖同此兩儀即同此太極置之
===
而塞焉者無間也純然貞一之義迄終古而常
行盖同此人心即同此生理溥之而横焉者無
極也施諸後世而何朝夕之有乎是則曾子之
有得于此而指其全體不息者語人也意深遠
矣抑孔子曰孝天之經也地之義也民之行也
天地之經而民實則之盖兼天下之理通天下
之情本其所得于天者然也以此博施濟衆位
天地而育萬物其孰能與於此哉其古之盡性
至命之聖者歟

于天直而立之不有以塞于天地乎四海亘隅
廣遠之極也孰能散而周之乎是孝也盖即其
太和之運而保合以有生凡所爲慈愛惻怛者

勢有泥而不行皆小道爾令也此然貞觀之道
歷萬世而無弊盖同此而施即□此□極置之
===
而塞焉者無閒也純然貞一之義延終古而常
行盖同此人心即同此生理溥之而横焉者無
極也施諸後世而何朝夕之有乎是則曾子之
有得于此而指其全體不息者語人也意深遠
矣抑孔子曰孝天之經也地之義也民之行也
天地之經而民實則之盖兼天下之理通天下
之情本其所得于天者然也以此博施濟衆位
天地而育萬物其孰能與於此哉其古之盡性
至命之聖者
punctuated:
也。盖即其生物之德而流行以爲命，凡所以敦化顯仁、盈兩間者，皆是也。所謂「發育萬物，峻極于天」，直而立之，不有以塞于天地乎？四海一隅，廣遠之極也。孰能散而周之乎？是孝也。盖即其太和之運而保合以有生，凡所爲慈愛惻怛者，舉天下皆然也。所謂「天下雷行，物與無妄」，敷而散之，不有以横于四海乎？然事有久而或弊，故勢有泥而不行，皆小道爾。今也，屹然貞觀之道，歷萬世而無弊。盖同此兩儀，即同此太極，置之而塞焉者無間也；純然貞一之義，迄終古而常行。盖同此人心，即同此生理，溥之而横焉者無極也。施諸後世，而何朝夕之有乎？是則曾子之有得于此，而指其全體不息者語人也，意深遠矣。
抑孔子曰：「孝，天之經也，地之義也，民之行也。天地之經，而民實則之。」盖兼天下之理，通天下之情，本其所得于天者然也。以此博施濟衆，位天地而育萬物，其孰能與於此哉？其古之盡性至命之聖者歟？
translation_en:
…it is filial piety. For it is precisely Heaven and Earth’s virtue of generating things, flowing forth to constitute their allotted nature and destiny. Everything that enriches transformation, manifests benevolence, and fills the space between Heaven and Earth is this. As the saying goes, “It fosters and nourishes the myriad things, and in its loftiness reaches Heaven.” Established upright, does it not thereby fill Heaven and Earth? The Four Seas, a single domain [?], represent the utmost breadth and distance. What can spread out and extend throughout them? It is filial piety. For it is precisely the operation of supreme harmony, preserving and uniting things so that they have life. All acts of loving kindness and compassionate concern are thus throughout the world. As the saying goes, “Thunder moves beneath Heaven; all things participate in freedom from falsehood.” Unfolding and spreading, does it not thereby extend across the Four Seas? Yet undertakings may deteriorate over time, and circumstances consequently become obstructed and cease to advance: these are all merely lesser ways. Here, however, the Way stands firm, constant and manifest, passing through ten thousand generations without deterioration. For sharing these same Two Modes—Heaven and Earth—means sharing this same Supreme Ultimate; established so as to fill them, it leaves no gap. The principle of pure constancy and unity continues to operate forever. For sharing this same human heart means sharing this same principle of life; diffused so as to extend everywhere, it has no limit. When applied to later generations, what distinction can there be between morning and evening? Thus Zengzi, having gained an understanding of this, pointed out to others its complete substance and ceaseless operation. His meaning is profound and far-reaching indeed.
Moreover, Confucius said: “Filial piety is the constant norm of Heaven, the proper principle of Earth, and the practice of the people. The people indeed take the constant norm of Heaven and Earth as their model.” It embraces all the principles of the world and comprehends all its feelings because it is rooted in what one has received from Heaven. Who could use this to confer benefits widely and aid the multitude, establish Heaven and Earth in their proper positions, and nourish the myriad things? Would it not be those sages of antiquity who fully realized their nature and attained their heavenly destiny?

Second Session
Discourse
“The Sage Can Establish Himself in a Position Free from Error”
Xu Renqing

Comment by Associate Examiner Su, Assistant Instructor: In writing a discourse, it is easy to elaborate, but difficult to be striking and distinguished; when discussing the learning of the mind, this is harder still. This essay alone displays outstanding insight and an antique elegance of expression and tone. It may be called the finest in the field.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: Writers are often constrained by the wording of the chapter on which the topic is based. They even borrow wholesale from the various chapters on “Observing Things,” thereby obscuring the true meaning instead. Late in the examination I came upon this script: its language is antique and its reasoning refined. Readers will return to it repeatedly; it should bring about a change in literary style.

Comment by Associate Examiner Cao, Instructor: Within writing governed by prescribed standards, extraordinary spirit and powerful talent are plainly evident. It far surpasses essays entangled in stale, conventional arguments or given to vague and irrelevant generalities.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Secretary: I read thirteen hundred discourse scripts in all. This essay is particularly well grounded in its arguments. It ranges freely through questions of the mind and human nature, saying whatever it wishes while never abandoning the proper standards. Its author must be a man of sustained self-cultivation and practical worth, not merely literary accomplishment—and how fine his writing is besides!

Comment by Examiner Peng, Right Mentor: This comes close to grasping the sage’s meaning.

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官侍講學士張批辭確義精蓋甞究心
於理學者
聖人所以大過人者無他焉亦惟心之純乎天
而已矣盖人生而靜天之性也動而未形幾也
幾弗審焉則天人判而過始萌矣聖人之心固
與夫人同也夫人救過且弗暇而聖人則粹然
以無疵何也盖極深研幾主乎靜而慎乎微其
寂也誠其感也神動靜無間天者弗違而渾然
無迹可見斯其所以大過于人而能立於無過
===
之地也聖人之能固夫人之所不能也盖亦淆
於靜而動以妄故失之遠復之難也是故言行
之過聖人弗憂也一念之微毫髮未盡有弗同
乎天者聖人之心缺然矣聖人之所以善事乎
心所以善事乎天也今夫過言由弗思也過動
由弗謀也顏氏弗貳不遠復也恒人過而知知
而悔悔而改者難矣而况於無過乎言行之無
過鮮矣而况於心乎且天下之事隱顯常變至
不一也而理則一理出於天而具於心者也使

聖人所以大過人者，無他焉，亦惟心之純乎天而已矣。盖人生而靜，天之性也；動而未形，幾也。幾弗審焉，則天人判而過始萌矣。聖人之心固與夫人同也。夫人救過且弗暇，而聖人則粹然以無疵，何也？盖極深研幾，主乎靜而慎乎微，其寂也誠，其感也神，動靜無間，天者弗違，而渾然無迹可見，斯其所以大過于人而能立於無過之地也。聖人之能，固夫人之所不能也。盖亦淆於靜而動以妄，故失之遠，復之難也。是故言行之過，聖人弗憂也。一念之微，毫髮未盡，有弗同乎天者，聖人之心缺然矣。聖人之所以善事乎心，所以善事乎天也。今夫過言由弗思也，過動由弗謀也。顏氏弗貳，不遠復也。恒人過而知，知而悔，悔而改者難矣，而况於無過乎？言行之無過鮮矣，而况於心乎？且天下之事，隱顯常變，至不一也；而理則一，理出於天而具於心者也。使
translation_en:
Examiner Zhang, Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “The language is precise and the meaning refined. The writer must have devoted himself to the study of principle.”

There is no other reason why the sage so greatly surpasses others: it is simply that his mind accords purely with Heaven. Human beings are still at birth: this is the nature imparted by Heaven. Movement that has not yet taken form is the incipient impulse. If this impulse is not carefully examined, Heaven and the human diverge, and error begins to sprout. The sage’s mind is fundamentally the same as that of others. Others scarcely have time even to remedy their errors, yet the sage remains pure and flawless. Why is this? He plumbs the depths and examines incipient impulses, grounding himself in stillness and exercising care over the slightest stirrings. In quiescence he is sincere; in responding to things he is spiritually discerning. There is no break between movement and stillness, no departure from Heaven, and all is an integral whole with no trace of effort to be seen. This is how he greatly surpasses others and can stand in a position free from error. What the sage can accomplish is indeed beyond the capacity of ordinary people. Their stillness is muddled, and their movement proceeds from delusion; thus they stray far, and returning is difficult.

Hence errors in speech and conduct are not what concern the sage. If, in the subtlety of a single thought, even the slightest imperfection remains—anything that does not accord with Heaven—the sage feels a deficiency in his heart. The way the sage attends well to his mind is the way he serves Heaven well. Errors in speech arise from failure to reflect; errors in action arise from failure to deliberate. Yan did not repeat his errors: he returned before straying far. For ordinary people, it is difficult to recognize an error, to regret it upon recognizing it, and to correct it upon regretting it. How much harder, then, to be without error! Freedom from error in speech and conduct is rare; how much rarer in the mind!

Moreover, the affairs of the world—hidden and manifest, constant and changing—are exceedingly diverse. Yet principle is one: it issues from Heaven and is fully present in the mind. If…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聖人不求之心而徒從事乎外則千蹊萬徑馳
騖不暇而吾身之過且叢然生矣所拂者益多
所補也益微吁聖人不若是之勞也所主一心
也心之靜而動天也天者理而已矣昔魯哀問
成身孔子曰不過乎物夫所謂物者心之實理
也是故寂然不動萬理具焉感而遂通萬理形
焉顯仁藏用善應而不窮曲成而不遺言而民
莫不信行而民莫不敬蓋有不言而信不動而
敬存乎其先曰是天也天也者聖人之所以協四
===
時道通鬼神者也語相發曰聖人曰聖人能立
無過之地惟從事於心也嗚呼邵子之言也有
自來矣堯舜授之也曰執中曰人心惟危道心
惟微惟精惟一開萬世無過之地也是故若湯
若高宗若武王若伊傅周公處時之迹雖異而
天下後世無異議焉者而論其治皆莫可及吁
盡其心純乎天而已矣至孔子從心不踰矩夫
不踰矩云者無過之謂也雖然衆人人矣聖人
之心純乎天矣未至聖者則天人之岐而聖賢

translation_en: …if the sage did not seek it within the mind but devoted himself solely to external things, he would have no respite from rushing along a thousand paths and ten thousand tracks, while faults would spring up thickly within himself. His transgressions would grow ever more numerous, and what he remedied would become ever more slight. Ah! The sage does not toil in this way: he takes the mind alone as his governing concern. The mind in stillness and in movement is Heaven; Heaven is nothing other than principle. Long ago, Duke Ai of Lu asked about perfecting oneself, and Confucius replied, “Do not err in relation to things.” Here, what are called “things” are the substantive principles within the mind. Thus, when it is quiescent and unmoving, the myriad principles are all present within it; when stimulated, it responds comprehensively, and the myriad principles become manifest. It makes benevolence visible while concealing its workings, responding aptly without exhaustion and bringing each thing to completion without omission. When the sage speaks, none among the people fail to trust him; when he acts, none fail to respect him. This is because, prior to these expressions, there already exists that which inspires trust without speech and respect without movement. This is called Heaven. Heaven is that through which the sage accords with the four seasons and, through the Way, communicates with ghosts and spirits. The sayings illuminate one another; the text says “sage” and then says [?]: “The sage can establish himself in a position free from error solely by applying himself to the mind.” Ah! Master Shao’s words have their origins. Yao and Shun transmitted this teaching, saying, “Hold fast to the Mean,” and “The human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle. Be discerning; be single-minded.” Thus they opened a realm free from error for all generations. Hence, such men as Tang, Gaozong, King Wu, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, and the Duke of Zhou differed in the courses they took in responding to their times, yet the world and later generations have raised no dissenting judgment about them; and, in assessing their government, none can equal them. Ah! They simply fully realized their minds and were wholly in accord with Heaven. As for Confucius, he followed his heart without overstepping the bounds. “Not overstepping the bounds” means being free from error. Nevertheless, ordinary people remain at the human level, while the sage’s mind is wholly in accord with Heaven. For those who have not yet attained sagehood, there is the divergence between Heaven and the human, and the distinction between sages and worthies…

…the boundary between sages and worthies lies precisely between having faults and being free of them. Thus, keeping his heart from departing from benevolence for three months was how Yan Hui aspired to sagehood. Alas, he attained this point, but did not live to complete its establishment! Yet how should one seek to reach this state? Master Zhou said to make stillness the guiding principle; Master Cheng spoke of reverent attentiveness; Master Zhu spoke of scrutinizing incipient stirrings. These are indeed where effort must be applied. If I can exert myself in these matters, the ground of freedom from faults will also be established within me. How could a sage be different from other people?

Examiner Peng, Right Mentor, comments: Its language resembles Yuanmo’s [?], while its feelings of loyalty and devotion are still more profound.
Examiner Zhang, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: Warm, generous, earnest, and sincere: it achieves the proper manner for addressing a sovereign.
We, your servants So-and-so and others, holding the designated offices, have reverently received the imperial instruction: “Because of the summer heat, suspend the lectures on the books for the time being; when autumn brings cooler weather, resume them as before.” Lofty and enlightened, Your Majesty follows the proper course, graciously accommodating what the Monthly Ordinances prescribe for the season. Abiding securely in profound stillness, you attend all the more closely to the admonition to heed the incipient workings of affairs at every moment. Ritual allows both tension and relaxation; learning requires continued illumination. We look forward to the next audience being not far distant and hope that your radiant understanding will continue to shine. Earnestly diligent and deeply devoted, we bow our heads to the ground and repeatedly kowtow.
We humbly consider that Fuxi’s delineation of Qian’s primal power teaches activity modeled on Heaven’s unceasing motion; the inscription on Tang’s basin teaches constant attention to Heaven’s mandate and daily renewal. To guard the mind, whose departures and returns have no fixed times, one must still rely on nurturing it at every instant. Thus loyal counsels carefully uphold the warning against indolence and neglect, while sagely learning initiates the transmission of the teaching to remain discerning and single-minded. Now we have reverently encountered Your Majesty, in whom reverence and frugality have become inherent qualities…

translation_en:
…Heaven has endowed Your Majesty with magnanimity and benevolence. You have inherited the imperial succession from three sages, and your beneficence reaches the nine regions. In attending upon the benevolent countenance of the Empress Dowager in Changle Palace, you have splendidly upheld filial devotion like Shun’s; in opening the lecture seats in Jinhua Hall, you have magnificently expounded plans for cultivated government. Diligent in hearing and reading, you extend the beginnings of goodness like a fire first kindled or a spring breaking forth. Unremitting in study and self-cultivation, you exalt consummate virtue through daily achievement and monthly progress. Having advanced so greatly in the work of becoming a sage, you are universally revered as the sovereign’s supreme exemplar.

As the sultry heat has just arrived, you have taken pity on the increased exertions of the assembled officials [?]. With still greater gracious consideration, you have suspended the lectures at the Classics Colloquium. We, your servants, hold posts together in the imperial library, yet our learning leaves us ashamed beside accomplished scholars. What do we know, and what can we do? We merely advance and withdraw with the others. Though temporarily deprived of attending your countenance at close quarters, we long to render even the smallest service. We fear that one day’s exposure to warmth may readily give way to cold, and reflect that every moment is precious.

For one’s resolve must be exacting in maintaining vigilance even when alone: anxious diligence guards against indolence and desire. Learning, meanwhile, requires concentrated application: recreation and rest assist inward cultivation and study. How could the comforts of leisure be allowed to fritter away time, fleeting as a colt glimpsed through a crack?

Formerly, your imperial ancestor had the Imperial Readings compiled during the Taiping era, and three fascicles were presented each day. Later, Renzong examined and recorded writings handed down from the past in Chongzheng Hall, going through all the classics within a year. These far-reaching plans would guide later generations; accounts of these splendid undertakings are still transmitted in…

punctuated: 中禁。及春秋之鼎盛，寧夙夜之豫康？朝野無虞，封章稀簡；穆清多暇，散帙煇煌。絃歌愠解於薫風，道義味延於永日。况睿資之天授，一覽盡乎精微；方聖敬之日躋，百物絶乎玩好。開卷自知其有益，建事惟求於多聞。伏願俯納輿言，式遵懿範，勤望道而若渴，懷慎徳以如氷。温故知新，餘事或兼乎翰墨；精義致用，往言必體諸心身。取左右逢其原，資深經史；念終始典於學，同古帝王。由兹不已之純，漸造無為之治。王猷允塞，丕圖永保於萬年；帝徳罔愆，鴻號獨煕乎千古。臣無任瞻天仰
translation_en:
…within the inner palace. While Your Majesty is in the prime of life, how could you rest in ease morning and night? Court and country are free of troubles, and sealed memorials are few and brief. In the august tranquility of the palace there is ample leisure to unfold the splendid books. As with song accompanied by strings in the fragrant southern breeze, resentment is dispelled; the savor of the Way and righteousness endures through the long days. Moreover, Your Majesty’s sagacious gifts are Heaven-bestowed: a single reading exhausts the subtlest meanings. Your sage reverence advances daily, and you reject all objects of idle amusement. In opening a book, you naturally recognize its benefit; in undertaking affairs, you seek only breadth of learning.

I humbly wish that you would graciously accept these public counsels and follow the excellent example of your predecessors. Diligently seek the Way as though thirsting for it, and cherish vigilance over your virtue as though treading on ice. Review the old to understand the new, perhaps devoting some remaining leisure to calligraphy and literary composition. Refine your understanding of principles and put them into practice, invariably embodying the words of the past in mind and person. Draw deeply upon the Classics and histories, finding the source wherever you turn; remember, from beginning to end, to make learning your constant rule, emulating the emperors and kings of antiquity. Through this unceasing purity of purpose, gradually attain government through nonaction. May the royal Way truly fill the realm, and the great imperial enterprise be preserved for ten thousand years. May imperial virtue be without error, and your exalted name shine uniquely through a thousand ages. Your servant cannot contain his feelings as he gazes toward Heaven and looks up toward…

translation_en:
…Your Sagely Majesty, with the utmost fervor and trembling apprehension, I respectfully submit this memorial for Your hearing.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions
First Question
Xu Renqing

Comment by Associate Examiner Su, Assistant Instructor: His examination and discussion of former dynasties, together with his account of the excellence of our Imperial Ancestor’s achievements, virtue, and institutional creations, unfold point upon point in orderly succession. He truly comprehends the deeper substance of past and present.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: His learning has a firm foundation, and his expansive vigor and majestic diction amply express it. Excellent in all three sessions, he fully merits a high recommendation.

Comment by Associate Examiner Cao, Instructor: Ranging freely through the classics and histories, he describes and discusses the flourishing institutions of our illustrious dynasty with boundless breadth, like the Yangtze and other great rivers rushing toward the sea. Wave upon wave rises, naturally forming a literary composition. He is indeed an outstanding talent of the southeast.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Secretary: Our dynasty has practiced benevolence through the generations [?]. Its rites and music, embodying equilibrium and harmony, have a foundation; yet the pitch standards for bells have not been fully investigated, as though awaiting someone. You range through past and present, fully exploring both underlying substance and formal expression, to contribute to the great undertaking. Your talent and insight are therefore already beyond the ordinary. Considered alongside the preceding two sessions and the following four policy essays, all are refined and erudite, with abundant vigor. In accordance with the usual practice, they are not all transcribed here.

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右諭德彭批歷代禮樂之制與我
聖祖所深望乎繼述者能鋪敘不遺且意見切當可備
聖明制作之助矣
考試官侍講學士張批能揄揚我
聖祖禮樂之盛且援古制作評品精當末復懇懇致望於
今日似有欲言未盡之意其嘗究心禮樂者乎
帝王之道大矣本之心身達之天下因天
地自然之序而禮以行因天地自然之和
而樂以作蓋志氣天人交相感應而雍熈
===
泰和之治所由成也苟推之無本行之非
時徒區區從事於儀文器數之間抑末矣
此我
皇祖禮樂之大同天地匹帝王而
超越之見尤慨漢文不能復古以寓
貽謀之深意也愚讀史記律書其始不言律
而言兵又於漢文加詳焉蓋偃兵息民天
下安樂斯可言制律爾班志曰至治之世
天地之氣合以生風風氣正十二律定非

translation_en:
Examiner Peng, Right Admonisher, comments: The institutions of ritual and music through successive dynasties, together with what our Sagely Ancestor earnestly expected of those who would carry on his work, are fully set forth without omission. Moreover, the views expressed are pertinent and sound, and may assist our sagacious sovereign in establishing institutions.

Examiner Zhang, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: The author ably extols the flourishing ritual and music of our Sagely Ancestor. He also draws upon ancient institutions, assessing them with precision and sound judgment. At the end, he again expresses earnest hopes for the present reign, seemingly with something still left unsaid. Has he not devoted himself to the study of ritual and music?

Great indeed is the Way of emperors and kings! It is rooted in the heart and person and extends throughout all under Heaven. Ritual is practiced in accordance with the natural order of Heaven and Earth; music is created in accordance with their natural harmony. Intent and vital energy, Heaven and humanity, respond to one another, and through this a reign of concord, prosperity, and supreme harmony is achieved. If its extension lacks a foundation and its practice is untimely, merely busying oneself with ceremonial forms and the specifications of instruments is surely to pursue only peripheral matters. Such was the greatness of our Imperial Ancestor’s ritual and music: it accorded with Heaven and Earth and matched that of ancient emperors and kings. His surpassing insight was especially evident in his regret that Emperor Wen of Han had failed to restore antiquity; therein lay his profound intention to bequeath guidance to his successors.

I have read the “Treatise on Pitch Standards” in the Records of the Grand Historian. At its beginning it discusses not pitch standards but warfare, and it treats Emperor Wen of Han in particular detail. For only when arms have been laid aside, the people given respite, and all under Heaven brought to peace and contentment can one speak of establishing pitch standards. title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
獨遷固言之子夏曰紀綱旣正天下大定
然後正律和聲弦歌詩頌此之謂德音周
子曰聖王制禮法修敎化三綱正九疇敘
百姓大和萬物咸若乃作樂以宣八風之
氣以平天下之情由斯言之在漢文亦未
足語此其唐虞三代乎盖自伏羲至黃帝
而五禮始備乃命伶倫制十二筩以聽鳳
鳴是爲律本堯德甚盛乃作大章然猶洪
水之方割也四凶之未去也及舜受禪重
===
華協載岳牧九官奮庸寅亮夔乃作樂神
人格鳳凰儀百獸率舞庶尹允諧垂二千
載且有觀於魯而興嘆聞於齊而忘味者
吁何盛哉大夏濩武固未逮也三代相因
禮可知已周公成文武之德監夏商之中
三千三百無不備焉夫樂盛於虞非德不
同旹未極也禮備於周非本之異文有加
也自魯兩生不行而漢之禮多襲秦陋藏
於理官雖高光功業庶幾可觀然詒謀未

punctuated: 獨遷固言之，子夏曰：「紀綱旣正，天下大定，然後正律和聲，弦歌詩頌，此之謂德音。」周子曰：「聖王制禮法，修敎化，三綱正，九疇敘，百姓大和，萬物咸若，乃作樂，以宣八風之氣，以平天下之情。」由斯言之，在漢文亦未足語此，其唐虞三代乎？盖自伏羲至黃帝而五禮始備，乃命伶倫制十二筩以聽鳳鳴，是爲律本。堯德甚盛，乃作大章，然猶洪水之方割也，四凶之未去也。及舜受禪，重華協載，岳牧九官奮庸寅亮，夔乃作樂，神人格，鳳凰儀，百獸率舞，庶尹允諧。垂二千載，且有觀於魯而興嘆、聞於齊而忘味者。吁，何盛哉！大夏、濩、武固未逮也。三代相因，禮可知已。周公成文武之德，監夏商之中，三千三百無不備焉。夫樂盛於虞，非德不同，旹未極也；禮備於周，非本之異，文有加也。自魯兩生不行，而漢之禮多襲秦陋，藏於理官。雖高光功業庶幾可觀，然詒謀未
translation_en:
…only Sima Qian and Ban Gu said this. Zixia said: “Once the guiding principles are set right and all under Heaven is firmly settled, only then should the pitch standards be rectified and the sounds harmonized, and the poems and hymns sung to stringed accompaniment. This is what is called the music of virtue.” Master Zhou said: “The sage kings established ritual and law and cultivated moral instruction. When the Three Bonds were correct, the Nine Categories properly ordered, the people in great harmony, and all things accorded with their nature, only then did they make music, to diffuse the vital energies of the eight winds and bring equilibrium to the feelings of all under Heaven.” Judging by these words, even Emperor Wen of Han was not yet sufficient to warrant speaking of such an achievement. Does it belong, then, to Tang and Yu—the ages of Yao and Shun—and the Three Dynasties?

From Fuxi down to the Yellow Emperor, the Five Rites only then became complete. The Yellow Emperor thereupon ordered Ling Lun to make twelve pitch pipes and listen to the phoenix’s call: this was the basis of the pitch standards. Yao’s virtue was exceedingly great, and he accordingly created the Great Manifestation music (Dazhang). Yet the flood was still wreaking havoc, and the Four Evildoers had not yet been removed. When Shun received the throne through abdication, his renewed brilliance joined that of Yao. The overseers of the sacred peaks, regional governors, and nine chief officials exerted themselves in service and assisted him with reverence. Kui then made music: spirits and humans arrived, phoenixes appeared in stately array, the hundred beasts all danced, and the various officials were truly in harmony. Nearly two thousand years later, there were still those who, seeing it performed in Lu, exclaimed in admiration, or hearing it in Qi, forgot the taste of food. Ah, how magnificent! The Great Xia music (Daxia), the Huo, and the Martial Dance (Wu) certainly did not equal it.

As the Three Dynasties inherited from one another, their rites can be known. The Duke of Zhou brought the virtue of Kings Wen and Wu to completion and took as his model the balanced practices of Xia and Shang. The three thousand detailed observances and three hundred principal rites were all fully provided for. That music flourished most under Yu does not mean that the virtue of the other rulers was different: its time had not yet reached its culmination. That ritual became complete under Zhou does not mean that its foundation differed: its outward forms had been augmented.

After the two scholars of Lu refused to go, Han ritual largely perpetuated the crude practices of Qin and was kept in the custody of judicial officials. Although the achievements of Emperors Gaozu and Guangwu were perhaps worthy of admiration, their plans bequeathed to posterity had not yet…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
善而治雜覇故制氏所傳鼓舞鏗鏘焉耳
河間所獻歳時備數焉耳况楚聲趙謳則
益侈矣所惜孝文謙讓未遑而仲舒王吉
劉向且汲汲於煩苛衰弱之世何益哉自
房杜不能對而唐之禮亦因隋舊雜以令
式雖貞觀開元庶幾乎治然閨門慙德而
治雜夷故七德武舞魏徵不視九代遺音
鄭衛不遠至霓裳羽衣則益荒矣盖太宗
以治忽不在樂而李義府許敬宗之徒又
===
多附會其何恠乎至宋大綱亦未見其能
正雖開寶而下言禮者莫不有撰述而郊
廟終未能一建隆之後制樂者非不求鐘
律而元聲迄未能定和峴以表定尺阮逸
以量求音胡瑗司馬光以尺生律而鑄工
必賂李照莫之辨房庶劉几以律生尺而
身為之度魏漢津尤可哂焉是皆出人為
智巧之私不協天地自然之氣誠有如我
皇祖所言者欲以動天地感鬼神豈不難哉嗚

以治忽不在樂而李義府許敬宗之徒又
===
多附會其何惟乎王朴大綱亦未見其能
正雖開寶而下言禮者莫不有撰述而郊
廟終未能一建隆之後制樂者非不求鐘
律而元聲迄未能定和峴以表定尺阮逸
以量求音胡瑗司馬光以尺生律而鑄工
又賂李照莫之辨房庶劉几以律生尺而
身爲之度魏漢津尤可哂焉是皆出人爲
智巧之私不協天地自然之氣誠有如我
皇祖所言者欲以動天地感鬼神豈不難哉嗚
punctuated: 善，而治雜覇，故制氏所傳，鼓舞鏗鏘焉耳；河間所獻，歳時備數焉耳。况楚聲趙謳，則益侈矣。所惜孝文謙讓未遑，而仲舒、王吉、劉向且汲汲於煩苛衰弱之世，何益哉？自房杜不能對，而唐之禮亦因隋舊，雜以令式。雖貞觀、開元庶幾乎治，然閨門慙德，而治雜夷，故七德武舞，魏徵不視；九代遺音，鄭衛不遠。至霓裳羽衣，則益荒矣。盖太宗以治忽不在樂，而李義府、許敬宗之徒又多附會，其何恠乎？至宋，大綱亦未見其能正。雖開寶而下，言禮者莫不有撰述，而郊廟終未能一；建隆之後，制樂者非不求鐘律，而元聲迄未能定。和峴以表定尺，阮逸以量求音，胡瑗、司馬光以尺生律，而鑄工必賂，李照莫之辨；房庶、劉几以律生尺，而身為之度，魏漢津尤可哂焉。是皆出人為智巧之私，不協天地自然之氣，誠有如我皇祖所言者。欲以動天地、感鬼神，豈不難哉？嗚
translation_en:
…sound, and their government was mixed with hegemonic practices. Thus what the Zhi family transmitted amounted merely to drumming, dancing, and the clang of instruments; what the Prince of Hejian presented merely filled out the required complement for seasonal observances. As for the sounds of Chu and the songs of Zhao, these were still more extravagant. Regrettably, Emperor Xiaowen, in his modesty and deference, never found time for this work, while Dong Zhongshu, Wang Ji, and Liu Xiang labored anxiously in an age of oppressive government and decline. What good could they do?

After Fang and Du proved unable to answer, Tang ritual likewise followed the old Sui practices, mingling them with administrative ordinances and regulations. Although the Zhenguan and Kaiyuan eras approached good government, there were shameful failings of virtue within the imperial household, and government was mixed with barbarian ways. Thus Wei Zheng would not watch the martial Dance of the Seven Virtues; and the surviving music of the nine ages was not far removed from the licentious music of Zheng and Wei. With Rainbow Skirts and Feathered Robes, the excesses grew still worse. Taizong held that good government and disorder did not depend on music, while men such as Li Yifu and Xu Jingzong frequently contrived arguments to suit his views. What is surprising about this?

By the Song, we still find no evidence that the fundamental framework had been set right. From the Kaibao era onward, everyone who discussed ritual produced writings, yet the rites of the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples were never unified. After the Jianlong era, those who established music certainly sought the proper bell pitches, yet the fundamental tone was never settled. He Xian used a gnomon to establish the standard foot; Ruan Yi sought musical tones through measures of capacity; Hu Yuan and Sima Guang derived the pitch standards from the standard foot. Yet the founders had to be bribed [?], and Li Zhao could not distinguish the discrepancies. Fang Shu and Liu Ji derived the standard foot from the pitch standards; as for using the body as a measure, Wei Hanjin was especially laughable.

All these methods arose from the private contrivances of human ingenuity and failed to accord with the natural qi of Heaven and Earth. They were indeed just as our imperial ancestor described. To seek through them to move Heaven and Earth and stir the ghosts and spirits—would that not be difficult? Alas…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
呼道喪千載胡元僭華自古所未有之大
變也重以大德泰定天曆之間綱常墜地
生民塗炭極矣洪惟我
太祖高皇帝膺
天眷命用夏變夷恢復文明之統蕩除腥穢之
風易冠裳於左衽拯水火而謳吟斯禮樂
之同天地者雖隆古莫及也况嚴
郊廟之祀肅
宮闈之禁觀心有亭精誠有錄君臣同遊即
===
===
虞廷都俞之風學士醉歌即成周鹿鳴之
雅斯禮樂之在心身者與古聖一揆也由
是達之天下正神祇之號均父母之服禁
兄弟之婚定上下之式采周官讀法以行
鄉社遵朱子家禮以令民間而禮行矣
大祀樂章則
親御宸藻大成樂器則頒習庠校命冷謙正
舞佾之位諭詹同製燕享之辭厭前代鄙
陋容悅之聲禁胡虜諠淫舞隊之戲而樂

translation_en:
…Alas! The Way had been lost for a thousand years. The barbarian Yuan’s usurpation of China was a great upheaval unprecedented since antiquity. Moreover, during the Dade, Taiding, and Tianli reign periods, the cardinal bonds and constant norms were cast to the ground, and the people’s suffering reached its utmost extremity. We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao received Heaven’s gracious mandate, transformed the barbarians through Chinese civilization, restored the succession of civilized rule, and swept away foul and defiling customs. He replaced left-lapped garments with proper caps and robes, rescuing the people from fire and water so that they sang his praises. Such ritual and music, in harmony with Heaven and Earth, surpassed even those of high antiquity.

Furthermore, he made solemn the sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temple and rigorously maintained the prohibitions of the inner palace. There was a pavilion for contemplating the mind and a record of utmost sincerity. The ruler and his ministers taking their leisure together embodied the spirit of the court of Shun, with its approving exchanges; the academicians singing in their cups embodied the refined spirit of “The Deer Cry” of the Zhou. Such ritual and music, embodied in mind and person, followed the same standard as the ancient sages. From these foundations he extended them throughout the realm: he corrected the titles of the deities, equalized mourning observances for fathers and mothers, prohibited marriage to a brother’s widow [?], and established ceremonial forms for superiors and inferiors. He adopted the practice of publicly reading the laws from the Offices of Zhou for implementation in village communities, and followed Master Zhu’s Family Rituals in issuing regulations for the common people. Thus ritual was put into practice.

For the musical texts of the great sacrifices, he personally wielded the imperial brush; instruments for the music honoring Confucius were distributed to the schools for practice. He ordered Leng Qian to rectify the positions of the ritual dance ranks and instructed Zhan Tong to compose lyrics for banquets. He rejected the crude and ingratiating music of former dynasties and prohibited the noisy, licentious performances of barbarian dance troupes, and music…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
正矣蓋自
開國已列局徵儒考訂於前繼又命牛諒陶
凱分掌於後今所輯大明集禮洪武禮制
諸書傳布服習已久惟鐘律之制聲容之
盛則未有纂述如虞之勸以九歌周大司
樂之敎國子者豈
聖慮未暇及乎蓋樂不可無因而强作氣必待
積久而後和伏讀
祖訓禁用肉刑戒伐遠夷重民命也載觀
===
大誥首敘同遊申明五常崇政敎也合而觀
之豈能無
深意於斯哉伏願
聖天子乘德位之隆弘繼述之孝由格致誠正
以為修齊治平之本由喜怒哀樂以致中
和位育之盛然後徧訪草澤大集文雅如
蔡元定之律呂新書朱子之通解鐘律可
考而知也如呂氏春秋通鑑外紀及隋志
所載黃鐘含少之數與朱蔡異者可按而

正矣。蓋自開國，已列局徵儒，考訂於前；繼又命牛諒、陶凱分掌於後。今所輯《大明集禮》《洪武禮制》諸書，傳布服習已久。惟鐘律之制、聲容之盛，則未有纂述，如虞之勸以九歌、周大司樂之敎國子者。豈聖慮未暇及乎？蓋樂不可無因而强作，氣必待積久而後和。伏讀《祖訓》，禁用肉刑，戒伐遠夷，重民命也；載觀《大誥》，首敘同遊，申明五常，崇政敎也。合而觀之，豈能無深意於斯哉？
伏願聖天子乘德位之隆，弘繼述之孝，由格致誠正以為修齊治平之本，由喜怒哀樂以致中和位育之盛。然後徧訪草澤，大集文雅。如蔡元定之《律呂新書》、朱子之《通解》，鐘律可考而知也；如《呂氏春秋》《通鑑外紀》及《隋志》所載黃鐘含少之數，與朱蔡異者，可按而
translation_en:
…was set right. From the founding of the dynasty, offices were established and Confucian scholars summoned to undertake examination and correction; subsequently, Niu Liang and Tao Kai were ordered to take separate charge of this work. The books compiled, including the Collected Rituals of the Great Ming and the Ritual System of the Hongwu Reign, have long circulated and been studied and put into practice. Only the system of bells and pitch standards and the flourishing forms of musical performance have yet to receive a comprehensive account comparable to Shun’s exhortation through the Nine Songs or the Zhou dynasty’s instruction of the sons of the state by the Music Master-in-chief. Could it be that the sagely sovereign had not yet found time to consider this? Music cannot be forcibly created without a foundation: vital forces must accumulate over a long period before attaining harmony. Humbly reading the Ancestral Instructions, I find prohibitions against mutilating punishments and warnings against attacking distant foreign peoples—expressions of concern for the lives of the people. Further examining the Grand Pronouncements, I find that it begins by describing “roaming together” [?] and elucidates the Five Constant Virtues, thereby exalting governance and moral instruction. Considered together, could these provisions fail to reveal a profound intention concerning this matter?
I humbly pray that Your Majesty, the sagely Son of Heaven, drawing upon your exalted virtue and position, will enlarge the filial devotion that continues and fulfills your ancestors’ undertakings. Make the investigation of things, extension of knowledge, sincerity of intentions, and rectification of the mind the foundation for cultivating the person, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to all under Heaven. Through joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, attain the fullness of equilibrium and harmony, whereby Heaven and Earth assume their proper places and all things flourish. Then seek widely among scholars outside official service and assemble a great company of learned men. From such works as Cai Yuanding’s New Treatise on the Pitch Standards and Master Zhu’s Comprehensive Explanations, the system of bells and pitch standards can be investigated and understood. title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
校也參度數之變求聲氣之元則與古帝
王異世同符而我
皇祖在天之靈所望於
聖子
神孫者亦可慰矣抑古者修禮樂以造士教中
和以防民誠不可一日廢者朱子嘗謂宜
立樂學久之則自有精通者出是亦一說
也愚敢以為
聖明獻
===
第二問
浦應麒
同考試官教諭潘批義嚴辭正末復歸
重於民而援引古君臣數語可以占所蘊矣
同考試官教諭林批祥異之策正以驗
忠悃爾是篇歷歷言之不矯不諛佳士也
同考試官署郎中丘批休咎雖殊惟修德
為本盖以人事天者當然也此作歷有發明而
忠愛之心溢言外矣

校也。參度數之變，求聲氣之元，則與古帝王異世同符，而我皇祖在天之靈所望於聖子神孫者，亦可慰矣。抑古者修禮樂以造士，教中和以防民，誠不可一日廢者。朱子嘗謂宜立樂學，久之則自有精通者出，是亦一說也。愚敢以為聖明獻。

第二問
浦應麒

同考試官教諭潘批：「義嚴辭正，末復歸重於民，而援引古君臣數語，可以占所蘊矣。」

同考試官教諭林批：「祥異之策，正以驗忠悃爾。是篇歷歷言之，不矯不諛，佳士也。」

同考試官署郎中丘批：「休咎雖殊，惟修德為本，盖以人事天者當然也。此作歷有發明，而忠愛之心溢言外矣。」
translation_en:
…and checked against one another. By examining variations in measures and numerical relations and seeking the source of sound and vital force (qi), Your Majesty would accord with the ancient sage kings, though living in a different age. The hopes that the spirit of our imperial ancestor in Heaven places in his sagely sons and divine grandsons could thus also be fulfilled. Moreover, the ancients cultivated ritual and music to train scholars and taught centrality and harmony to restrain the people: these truly cannot be neglected for even a single day. Master Zhu once said that a school of music should be established, and that, in time, people thoroughly versed in it would naturally emerge. This, too, is a proposal worth considering. I humbly venture to offer it to Your Sagely Majesty.

Second Question
Pu Yingqi

Comment by Associate Examiner Pan, Instructor: “The principles are rigorous and the language upright. At the end, he again places the emphasis on the people. The several sayings he cites from ancient rulers and ministers allow us to discern the understanding he possesses.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: “A policy question on auspicious signs and anomalies serves precisely to test sincere loyalty. This essay discusses them clearly and distinctly, neither feigning conviction nor offering flattery. He is a worthy scholar.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Qiu, Acting Bureau Director: “Although favorable and unfavorable portents differ, cultivating virtue alone is fundamental. This is indeed the proper way to serve Heaven through human affairs. This composition offers illuminating explanations throughout, and a heart filled with loyalty and devotion is evident beyond its words.”

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右諭德彭批灾祥之對能究極天
人之微略無諛辭而儆戒交修之意惓至是可
錄也
考試官侍講學士張批能道數千年灾祥得
失之故又惓惓以上下交儆爲言其有忠
君愛國之忱者乎
人君之事天也猶事親也人臣之事君也
猶事天也知所以事親則知所以事天矣
知所以事天則知所以事君矣盖親有喜
怒皆不爲不愛其子天有祥異皆不爲不
愛其君君以是修德而飭乎下臣以是修
職而弼乎上皆無所不用其誠敬斯交儆
相成之道祈天永命之本也是故祥多而
恃未必不危異眾而戒未必不安顧人應
之何如耳此張子西銘所謂大君吾父母
宗子大臣吾宗子家相真西山所謂知父
母之心可以知天心知人君之道可以知
天道之說也執事豈不有見乎此而猶下

translation_en:
Examiner Peng, Right Mentor, comments: This response concerning calamities and auspicious signs thoroughly explores the subtleties of the relationship between Heaven and humanity, without the slightest flattery. Its concern for mutual admonition and cultivation is deeply earnest. It merits selection.

Examiner Zhang, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: He can explain the causes of calamities and auspicious signs, successes and failures, over several thousand years. Moreover, he earnestly urges those above and below to admonish one another. Surely he possesses heartfelt loyalty to his ruler and love for his country!

A ruler serves Heaven as he serves his parents; a minister serves his ruler as he serves Heaven. Knowing how to serve one’s parents, one knows how to serve Heaven; knowing how to serve Heaven, one knows how to serve one’s ruler. Parents may be pleased or angry, but neither means that they do not love their children. Heaven may send auspicious signs or anomalies, but neither means that it does not love its ruler. Through these, the ruler cultivates his virtue and admonishes those below, while ministers attend diligently to their duties and assist the one above. All apply their sincerity and reverence in everything. This is the way of mutual admonition and assistance toward fulfillment, and the foundation for praying to Heaven for an enduring Mandate. Thus, relying complacently on numerous auspicious signs does not ensure freedom from danger; taking warning from numerous anomalies does not preclude security. It depends only on how people respond to them. This is what Master Zhang means in the Western Inscription (Ximing): “The great ruler is the principal heir of my parents; the great ministers are the household stewards of that heir.” It is also what Zhen Xishan means when he says: “By knowing the hearts of parents, one can know Heaven’s heart; by knowing the way of a ruler, one can know Heaven’s way.” Have you, honored examiners, not already perceived this, and yet condescend to…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
詢承學無亦因事納忠以寓持盈保終之
意歟雖然天人之際未易言也稱洪範庶
徵則堯湯有水旱之灾稱禮運四靈則五
代多麟鳳龜龍之屬以文景之賢而彗孛
地震山崩水潰之異史不絕書以武宣之
世而芝房寶鼎神爵甘露往往紀年而歌
詠是誠不可一端求也故漢儒向歆仲舒
京房翼奉之徒或采春秋以附時事或析
福極以配五行皆未免旁引曲證而失之
===
鑿頓以啟人主不足信之疑如歐陽氏鄭
夾漈之論則又以四靈為非瑞以五行為
妖妄亦未免矯枉過正而失之疎適以導
人臣不足畏之佞惟孔子作春秋不書慶
祥則懼夫人之偶同而或恃以驕也其紀
灾異不著事應則懼夫人之偶異而或忽
以怠也稽之往古伏羲龍師而龍名少皥
鳥師而鳥名民事尚畧取諸遠爾至於受
河圖而八卦畫受洛書而九疇敘盖仰觀

punctuated: 詢承學，無亦因事納忠，以寓持盈保終之意歟？雖然，天人之際未易言也。稱《洪範》庶徵，則堯、湯有水旱之灾；稱《禮運》四靈，則五代多麟鳳龜龍之屬。以文景之賢，而彗孛、地震、山崩、水潰之異，史不絕書；以武宣之世，而芝房、寶鼎、神爵、甘露，往往紀年而歌詠。是誠不可一端求也。故漢儒向、歆、仲舒、京房、翼奉之徒，或采《春秋》以附時事，或析福極以配五行，皆未免旁引曲證而失之鑿，頓以啟人主不足信之疑。如歐陽氏、鄭夾漈之論，則又以四靈為非瑞，以五行為妖妄，亦未免矯枉過正而失之疎，適以導人臣不足畏之佞。惟孔子作《春秋》，不書慶祥，則懼夫人之偶同而或恃以驕也；其紀灾異，不著事應，則懼夫人之偶異而或忽以怠也。稽之往古，伏羲龍師而龍名，少皥鳥師而鳥名，民事尚畧，取諸遠爾。至於受河圖而八卦畫，受洛書而九疇敘，盖仰觀
translation_en:
…consult a student of the received learning: might your intention also be to use this occasion to invite loyal counsel, with a view to preserving prosperity and securing a good end? Even so, the relationship between Heaven and humanity is not easily discussed. If we invoke the various signs described in the Great Plan, there were still disastrous floods and droughts under Yao and Tang. If we invoke the four numinous creatures described in the Evolution of Rites, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and dragons appeared frequently during the Five Dynasties. Despite the worthiness of Emperors Wen and Jing, the histories record an unbroken succession of anomalies: comets, earthquakes, collapsing mountains, and overflowing waters. Yet in the reigns of Emperors Wu and Xuan, auspicious fungi, precious tripods, divine birds, and sweet dew repeatedly furnished names for reign periods and subjects for songs of praise. These matters truly cannot be understood from a single perspective.

Thus Han scholars such as Liu Xiang, Liu Xin, Dong Zhongshu, Jing Fang, and Yi Feng either drew on the Spring and Autumn Annals to make connections with contemporary events, or analyzed blessings and calamities to correlate them with the Five Phases. None escaped drawing on remote parallels and straining evidence, falling into forced interpretations and thereby [?] prompting rulers to doubt whether such things deserved belief. Arguments such as those of Master Ouyang and Zheng Jiaji, however, held that the four numinous creatures were not auspicious signs and that interpretations based on the Five Phases were superstitious falsehoods. These likewise went too far in correcting error and became excessively dismissive, serving only to encourage ministers in the sycophantic claim that such things need not be feared.

Confucius alone, in composing the Spring and Autumn Annals, omitted felicitous and auspicious signs, fearing that people might rely on an accidental correspondence and grow arrogant. When recording calamities and anomalies, he did not identify the events to which they corresponded, fearing that people might disregard them and become negligent because of an accidental discrepancy. Looking back into remote antiquity, Fuxi arranged his officials under the sign of the dragon and gave them dragon names; Shaohao arranged his officials under the sign of birds and gave them bird names. The administration of the people was still rudimentary, and they merely drew their models from things remote from human affairs. As for receiving the River Chart and drawing the Eight Trigrams, and receiving the Luo Writing and setting out the Nine Categories, these surely involved looking upward to observe…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
俯察因象數以成天下之務以冒天下之
道非有言語文字如後世也洚水儆予堯
以為憂而舜禹是用萬世且永賴矣桑林
之禱湯以為憂而君臣一德六事且自責
矣若虞稱儀鳳而敕天之歌惓惓乎時幾
之謹周載嘉禾而無逸之訓惓惓乎稼穡
之難則上下之交儆可知也文景承干戈
甫定之餘躬修玄默敦尚儉朴其臣又多
重厚長者故今年詔勸農桑明年詔減田
===
租陳武征伐之請賈生禮樂之議皆有未
遑雖天杯寶鼎晚年少惑而新垣平之誅
其復不遠是以戶口蕃息斷獄數百災異
雖眾亦何足累哉武宣當國家富庶之後
才高志廣好大喜功其臣類多文過其實
故一物之異即升樂府一瑞之上輒用改
元仲舒正心之策汲黯多欲之戒皆不見
用雖白四方災異可謂賢相而宋疇之駁
亦不能救是以海內困窮幾續亡秦祥瑞

遑雖再杯寳鼎晚年少惑而新垣平之誅
其復不遠是以戶口蕃息斷獄數百災異

punctuated: 俯察，因象數以成天下之務，以冒天下之道，非有言語文字如後世也。「洚水儆予」，堯以為憂，而舜禹是用，萬世且永賴矣。桑林之禱，湯以為憂，而君臣一德，六事且自責矣。若虞稱儀鳳，而敕天之歌惓惓乎時幾之謹；周載嘉禾，而《無逸》之訓惓惓乎稼穡之難，則上下之交儆可知也。文景承干戈甫定之餘，躬修玄默，敦尚儉朴，其臣又多重厚長者。故今年詔勸農桑，明年詔減田租，陳武征伐之請、賈生禮樂之議，皆有未遑。雖天杯寶鼎，晚年少惑，而新垣平之誅，其復不遠。是以戶口蕃息，斷獄數百，災異雖眾，亦何足累哉？武宣當國家富庶之後，才高志廣，好大喜功，其臣類多文過其實。故一物之異，即升樂府；一瑞之上，輒用改元。仲舒正心之策、汲黯多欲之戒，皆不見用。雖白四方災異，可謂賢相，而宋疇之駁亦不能救。是以海內困窮，幾續亡秦，祥瑞
translation_en:
…and observing below, they used images and numbers to accomplish the affairs of all under Heaven and encompass its principles; there were no spoken or written formulations such as those of later ages. “The floodwaters warn me”: Yao took this as cause for concern and employed Shun and Yu, upon whom countless generations would depend forever. In his prayer at Sanglin, Tang likewise expressed his concern; ruler and ministers shared a single virtue, and he reproached himself on six counts. Although the age of Yu celebrated the phoenix coming to display its stately bearing, the song urging attentiveness to Heaven earnestly stressed vigilance over the subtle beginnings of events. Although the Zhou recorded auspicious grain, the admonitions in Against Ease earnestly stressed the hardships of sowing and reaping. From this we can see how those above and below warned one another.

Emperors Wen and Jing came to power when warfare had only just subsided. They personally cultivated quiet noninterference and earnestly valued frugality and simplicity; their ministers, too, were mostly sober, substantial men of mature judgment. Thus, one year they issued an edict encouraging agriculture and sericulture, and the next an edict reducing the land tax. They had no time to take up either Chen Wu’s request for military campaigns or Master Jia’s proposals concerning rites and music. Although the heavenly cup [?] and precious tripod somewhat deluded Emperor Wen in his later years, the execution of Xinyuan Ping showed that he returned to the proper course before straying far. Consequently, households and population multiplied, and criminal cases adjudicated numbered only in the hundreds. Though disasters and anomalies were numerous, how could they detract from these achievements?

Emperors Wu and Xuan ruled after the state had become wealthy and prosperous. Highly talented and ambitious, they delighted in grand undertakings and coveted achievements; their ministers, for the most part, possessed more outward polish than substance. Thus, whenever an unusual creature appeared, it was immediately celebrated through the Music Bureau; whenever an auspicious portent was presented, it prompted a change of reign title. Neither Dong Zhongshu’s policy proposal on rectifying the ruler’s mind nor Ji An’s warning against excessive desires was adopted. Although the minister who reported disasters and anomalies throughout the realm could be called a worthy Counsellor-in-Chief, even Song Chou’s rebuttal [?] could not remedy matters. Consequently, all within the seas suffered destitution, and the dynasty nearly followed the fallen Qin. As for the auspicious portents…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之集其矯誣也哉玄宗初年銳意於治觀
其獻瑞應圖則曰春秋不書祥瑞惟記有
年一何明也曲江罷而靈符出天寶之號
改矣雖漁陽之變不克有終說者謂自封
禪之請日食不虧之賀其漸已久末流尚
可防乎眞宗初年政從簡易觀其獻嘉禾
則曰天下豐稔即爲祥瑞又著論以示羣
臣一何慎也文靖沒而天書下祥符之事
多矣雖澶淵之恥有爲口實說者謂美珠
===
之賜乾佑之進賢者且然其他又何責乎
由是觀之君臣交修雖灾亦治君臣少肆
雖祥亦亂天豈遠乎人哉方今
聖天子憂勤于上同符帝王而諸大臣將順於
下遠鑒唐宋是以聞祥瑞而不賀遇灾變
而致謹是深有得於春秋之義自足以折
諸儒之論矣抑愚竊謂敬
天之實豈有他哉無亦盡心於民斯可矣觀禹
陳吉凶影響之謨而曰善政養民□□□

之集，其矯誣也哉！玄宗初年，銳意於治。觀其獻瑞應圖，則曰：「春秋不書祥瑞，惟記有年。」一何明也！曲江罷而靈符出，天寶之號改矣。雖漁陽之變，不克有終，說者謂自封禪之請、日食不虧之賀，其漸已久，末流尚可防乎？眞宗初年，政從簡易。觀其獻嘉禾，則曰：「天下豐稔，即爲祥瑞。」又著論以示羣臣，一何慎也！文靖沒而天書下，祥符之事多矣。雖澶淵之恥，有爲口實，說者謂美珠之賜、乾佑之進，賢者且然，其他又何責乎？
由是觀之，君臣交修，雖灾亦治；君臣少肆，雖祥亦亂。天豈遠乎人哉！方今聖天子憂勤于上，同符帝王，而諸大臣將順於下，遠鑒唐宋。是以聞祥瑞而不賀，遇灾變而致謹，是深有得於春秋之義，自足以折諸儒之論矣。抑愚竊謂敬天之實，豈有他哉？無亦盡心於民斯可矣。觀禹陳吉凶影響之謨，而曰：「善政養民。」□□□
translation_en:
…the gathering of auspicious signs—was it not fabrication and deception? In the early years of Xuanzong’s reign, he devoted himself earnestly to good government. Consider his response when presented with a Chart of Auspicious Portents: “The Spring and Autumn Annals does not record auspicious signs; it records only years of good harvests.” How discerning he was! Yet once Qujiang [Zhang Jiuling] was dismissed, a numinous talisman appeared, and the reign title was changed to Tianbao. Although the rebellion at Yuyang meant that he failed to bring his reign to a good conclusion, commentators maintain that the slide had long since begun, with the request to perform the feng and shan sacrifices and the congratulations offered when a predicted solar eclipse did not occur. Could its final consequences still have been prevented?
In the early years of Zhenzong’s reign, government followed principles of simplicity and ease. Consider his response when presented with auspicious grain: “Abundant harvests throughout the realm are themselves auspicious signs.” He also composed a discourse to show his assembled ministers. How circumspect he was! Yet once Wenjing [Li Hang] died, a heavenly writing descended, and affairs involving auspicious talismans multiplied. Although the humiliation at Chanyuan furnished a pretext, commentators point to the gift of fine pearls and Qianyou’s advancement [?]: if even the worthy behaved thus, what could one demand of the others?
Viewed in this light, when ruler and ministers cultivate themselves together, there is good government even amid calamities; when ruler and ministers become even slightly unrestrained, there is disorder even amid auspicious signs. How could Heaven be remote from human affairs? Today our sagely Son of Heaven labors anxiously above, matching the exemplary emperors and kings, while the great ministers below support and carry forward his intentions, taking warning from the distant examples of the Tang and Song. Thus, on hearing of auspicious signs, they offer no congratulations; on encountering calamities and anomalies, they exercise utmost caution. This shows a profound grasp of the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals and is sufficient in itself to refute the arguments of the various scholars. Yet I venture, in my ignorance, to suggest: can the substance of reverence for Heaven consist in anything else? Surely devoting oneself wholeheartedly to the people is enough. Consider how Yu set forth his counsel that good and ill fortune follow conduct as shadows and echoes follow their sources, saying: “Good government nourishes the people.” [Three illegible characters] …

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
聰明明畏之謨而曰安民則惠天命降監
下民有嚴商之所以頌高宗也上下勤恤
欲王以小民受天永命召公之所以告成
王也何者君受命於天臣受命於君凡以
爲民而已舍人事而徴天道有是理哉一
得之愚誠無出此惟執事敎之幸甚
第三問
皇甫涍
同考試官敎諭林批五策至周禮率難
===
分析是篇獨條答且折衷以朱子之論故錄之
同考試官敎諭林批議論辯析皆有根
據如子言周禮可行矣不但博洽而已也
同考試官主事余批周禮一書綱目畢
舉非聖人莫之作答者殊無定見子能悉之可
與言治矣
考試官右諭德彭批周禮之疑對者未半
率騁浮辭填塞此卷五策出入經史已迥出人
右錄此則餘可知矣

聰明明畏之謨，而曰：「安民則惠。」天命降監，下民有嚴，商之所以頌高宗也；上下勤恤，欲王以小民受天永命，召公之所以告成王也。何者？君受命於天，臣受命於君，凡以爲民而已。舍人事而徴天道，有是理哉？一得之愚，誠無出此，惟執事敎之，幸甚。
第三問
皇甫涍
同考試官敎諭林批：「五策至周禮，率難分析。是篇獨條答，且折衷以朱子之論，故錄之。」
同考試官敎諭林批：「議論辯析皆有根據。如子言，周禮可行矣，不但博洽而已也。」
同考試官主事余批：「周禮一書，綱目畢舉，非聖人莫之作。答者殊無定見，子能悉之，可與言治矣。」
考試官右諭德彭批：「周禮之疑，對者未半，率騁浮辭填塞。此卷五策出入經史，已迥出人右。錄此，則餘可知矣。」
translation_en:
…the counsel concerning Heaven’s hearing and sight, its making manifest and inspiring awe, says: “Bring peace to the people, and you will accord with Heaven.” Heaven’s mandate descends in scrutiny, and the people below are to be held in awe: this is how the Shang hymned Gaozong. Those above and below must diligently care for the people, so that the king may, through the common people, receive Heaven’s enduring mandate: this is how the Duke of Shao admonished King Cheng. Why is this so? The ruler receives his mandate from Heaven, and ministers receive their mandates from the ruler, all solely for the people’s sake. Could it make sense to set aside human affairs and seek evidence of the Way of Heaven? My humble insight truly goes no further than this. I would be most fortunate to receive your instruction.
Third Question
Huangfu Xiao
Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: “In the five policy essays, when candidates reach the Rites of Zhou, they generally find it difficult to analyze. This essay alone answers point by point and weighs the issues against Master Zhu’s arguments. Therefore it has been selected.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: “The arguments and distinctions are all well grounded. On your account, the Rites of Zhou could indeed be put into practice. This is more than merely extensive learning.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Secretary: “The Rites of Zhou comprehensively sets forth both its main principles and their particulars. None but a sage could have composed it. Those answering have notably lacked settled views. You understand it thoroughly and are someone with whom one can discuss government.”
Comment by Examiner Peng, Right Mentor: “Not even half the candidates address the doubts concerning the Rites of Zhou; most give free rein to empty phrases to fill the space. The five policy essays in this examination script range through the classics and histories and already stand far above those of others. Selecting this one suffices to convey the quality of the rest.”

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官侍講學士張批世之談經者往往致
疑周禮故大經大法率廢而不講是作獨以聖
人之心爲言可謂知本之論矣
知聖人之心於千載之上而後可以談經
得聖人之心於千載之下而後可以致治
夫不得其心而徒泥其跡則言之者失之
固固則廢行之者失之疎疎則弊其廣大
之規精微之蘊乃始弗見於天下矣况未
經孔子之論定孟子諸儒之弼承而後世
===
之疑愈甚吁疑其小而並廢其大豈不深
可慨哉執事以周禮下策承學愚也非敢
自謂知聖人之心而有得也然亦嘗致力
於是矣請試陳之夫王者之制莫備於周
禮盖周公成文武之德而畫爲萬世之經
其建官以三百六十其兵農以井田其取
民以什一其教民以鄉遂其養士以學校
其治天下以封建其威民以肉刑大本旣
立然後隨而增益之上則六典八法八則

punctuated:

知聖人之心於千載之上，而後可以談經；得聖人之心於千載之下，而後可以致治。夫不得其心而徒泥其跡，則言之者失之固，固則廢；行之者失之疎，疎則弊。其廣大之規、精微之蘊，乃始弗見於天下矣。况未經孔子之論定、孟子諸儒之弼承，而後世之疑愈甚。吁！疑其小而並廢其大，豈不深可慨哉！執事以周禮下策，承學愚也，非敢自謂知聖人之心而有得也，然亦嘗致力於是矣。請試陳之。夫王者之制，莫備於周禮。盖周公成文武之德，而畫爲萬世之經。其建官以三百六十，其兵農以井田，其取民以什一，其教民以鄉遂，其養士以學校，其治天下以封建，其威民以肉刑。大本旣立，然後隨而增益之。上則六典、八法、八則
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Expositor-in-Waiting: Those who discuss the classics today often cast doubt upon the Rites of Zhou; consequently, its great principles and fundamental institutions are largely set aside without discussion. This essay alone makes the mind of the sage its central concern. It may indeed be called an argument that understands the foundation.

Only by understanding the mind of the sage who lived a thousand years before us can we discuss the classics; only by grasping that mind a thousand years after his time can we bring about good government. If people fail to grasp his mind and merely cling to the traces he left, those who expound them err through rigidity, and rigidity leads to their abandonment; those who implement them err through laxity, and laxity leads to abuses. Thus the vast scope of his designs and the subtle depths of his thought cease to be manifest in the world. Moreover, the Rites of Zhou did not undergo Confucius’s critical determination or receive the supporting transmission of Mencius and the other scholars, and later generations’ doubts grew still greater. Alas! To doubt its minor points and discard its major principles along with them—is this not deeply lamentable? You, honored examiners, have set a policy question on the Rites of Zhou. I am a foolish student and dare not claim that I understand the sage’s mind or have grasped its meaning; yet I have devoted effort to this subject. Allow me to attempt an exposition.

Among the institutions of true kings, none are more complete than those in the Rites of Zhou. The Duke of Zhou brought the virtue of Kings Wen and Wu to fulfillment and laid out an enduring norm for all ages. He established 360 offices; organized soldiers and farmers through the well-field system; levied a tithe upon the people; instructed them through the xiang and sui administrative districts; nurtured scholars through schools; governed the realm through enfeoffment; and awed the people through corporal punishments. Once this great foundation had been established, he added further provisions accordingly. At the highest level were the Six Canons, Eight Regulations, and Eight Rules…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
九柄九貢九賦九式之序次則祭祀朝覲
冠昏喪紀師田行役之詳下至車旗圭璧
之器梓匠輪輿之度與夫畫績搏埴之法
又其細及魚虫之微至纖至悉無不畢具
而意之所在雖六卿各分其職而大宰得
總其權維時道洽政治四方無虞固本於
關雎麟趾之化而法度之維持者亦不可
誣也故鄭玄以為周公致大平之跡仲長
統亦謂周禮為禮記之經皆有見矣若攷
===
其時則賈公彥以為六年所制得之而鄭
衆謂作之於豐者失矣挾書之律既除河
間獻王得之李氏乃始入於秘府劉歆見
而重之鄭緱杜賈各為疏解乃徧授於諸
儒即設位言之謂之周官即制作言之謂
之周禮劉歆嘗奏置博士矣而因格於兵
荒武帝嘗欲設學官矣而為羣疑所沮其
與王制不合者盖王制之言出漢儒掇拾
之餘與軻書不同者盖孟氏之論在諸侯

九柄、九貢、九賦、九式之序；次則祭祀、朝覲、冠昏、喪紀、師田、行役之詳；下至車旗、圭璧之器，梓匠、輪輿之度，與夫畫績、搏埴之法，又其細及魚虫之微，至纖至悉，無不畢具。而意之所在，雖六卿各分其職，而大宰得總其權。維時道洽政治，四方無虞，固本於《關雎》《麟趾》之化，而法度之維持者亦不可誣也。故鄭玄以為周公致大平之跡，仲長統亦謂《周禮》為《禮記》之經，皆有見矣。若攷其時，則賈公彥以為六年所制，得之；而鄭衆謂作之於豐者，失矣。
挾書之律既除，河間獻王得之李氏，乃始入於秘府。劉歆見而重之，鄭緱杜賈各為疏解，乃徧授於諸儒。即設位言之，謂之《周官》；即制作言之，謂之《周禮》。劉歆嘗奏置博士矣，而因格於兵荒；武帝嘗欲設學官矣，而為羣疑所沮。其與《王制》不合者，盖《王制》之言出漢儒掇拾之餘；與軻書不同者，盖孟氏之論在諸侯
translation_en:
…the ordering of the nine instruments of authority, nine categories of tribute, nine categories of taxation, and nine standards of expenditure; next, the particulars of sacrifices, court audiences, capping ceremonies and marriages, mourning observances, military expeditions and hunts, and journeys on official service; and further down, the equipment of chariots and banners, jade tablets and disks, the specifications for woodworkers, wheelwrights, and carriage makers, and the methods of painting, spinning, and molding clay. Its finer details extend even to such minute creatures as fish and insects: nothing, however subtle or particular, is omitted. Its underlying intention was that, although the Six Ministers each had their separate responsibilities, the Grand Steward should wield overall authority. At that time, the Way prevailed, government was well ordered, and the four quarters were free of troubles. This was certainly rooted in the moral transformation exemplified by “The Ospreys” (Guanju) and “The Qilin’s Hoofs” (Linzhi), yet the sustaining role of laws and institutions cannot be denied. Thus Zheng Xuan regarded it as the record of how the Duke of Zhou achieved great peace, while Zhongchang Tong likewise called the Rites of Zhou the guiding framework of the Book of Rites. Both judgments show insight. As for its date, Jia Gongyan was correct in considering it a work of the sixth year of the Duke of Zhou’s regency; Zheng Zhong was mistaken in saying it was composed at Feng.
After the law prohibiting possession of books was abolished, Prince Xian of Hejian obtained it from the Li family, and only then did it enter the imperial repository. Liu Xin saw it and valued it highly. Zheng, Gou, Du, and Jia [?] each supplied explanatory commentaries, and it then came to be widely transmitted among scholars. In terms of its establishment of official positions, it is called the Offices of Zhou; in terms of its creation of institutions, it is called the Rites of Zhou. Liu Xin once petitioned to establish Erudites for its study, but warfare and famine obstructed the proposal. Emperor Wu once intended to establish academic officials for it, but widespread doubts thwarted him. Where it disagrees with the “Royal Regulations,” this is because the statements in the “Royal Regulations” derive from materials pieced together by Han scholars. Where it differs from the book of Meng Ke, this is because Master Meng’s discussions came after the feudal lords…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
去籍之後冬官之屬雜見於五官之中要
之不全若强續所不類猶以羔補狐以縞
補緇適所以致疑凡可疑者皆此類也五
官之缺如嗇夫司商之類不見亡於秦火
若强以為全不知儀禮所載國語所錄自
足以相證凡所闕者亦此類也設官分職
周書舉其槩周禮盡其詳因事以存名要
之分攝者多固不一一求備爾遂人匠人
一以長言之一以广言之因地以順其勢
===
故其縱橫有不同均之以便民爾內宰之
掌固有寺人女史之屬凡奔走趨事與敎
灋之備者皆其為之宰特主其職耳而六
宫嬪御祼獻瑶爵佐后立市皆禮之宜有
者也豈若後世之婦無功事而祭獻不聞
者乎三物之法求其德行道藝之全鄉大
夫受敎灋於司徒退而頒之於鄉吏使各
以敎其所治登其夫家之衆寡三年大比
賓之於王所謂使民興賢出使長之使民

Forcibly supplementing it with material of a different kind would be like patching fox fur with lambskin, or black silk with white silk: it would only give rise to doubts. All the doubtful points are of this kind. As for omissions in the five ministries, offices such as the sefu and the sishang [?] are absent, having been lost in the Qin burning of books. Anyone who insists that the text is complete fails to recognize that the accounts in the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili) and the Discourses of the States (Guoyu) suffice to corroborate one another. The omissions, too, are all of this kind.

As for establishing offices and assigning duties, the Documents of Zhou (Zhou shu) gives their general outline, while the Rites of Zhou (Zhou li) sets out their details. Titles were preserved according to the tasks concerned; in sum, many duties were divided among officials or performed concurrently, so a complete correspondence cannot be demanded in every instance. Of the Director of the Outer Suburbs and the master craftsmen, one speaks in terms of length and the other in terms of breadth [?]. Each follows the configuration of the terrain; hence their longitudinal and transverse arrangements differ, but both serve the people's convenience.

Under the Palace Steward there were indeed such personnel as eunuch attendants and female scribes. They performed all the errands and services and carried out the full provisions for instruction and regulation; the Steward merely presided over their duties. The consorts and attendants of the six palaces, libations and offerings with jade cups, and assisting the queen in establishing the market are all things properly provided for by ritual. How could this resemble later ages, when women have no productive duties and nothing is heard of their participation in sacrificial offerings?

text:
興能入使治之而亦未嘗求備也豈若後
世之徇名取士而行業無聞者乎屬民讀
法非擾也於民彌親故教彌數而民日遷
於善矣廛人五布非苛也抑其逐末作之
務本而民浮偽自消矣以國服為息如農
以粟米工以器械隨所有以為便非稱貸
以取償亦何近利之有賈田掌於載師者
盖吏為縣官所鬻而非商賈所受四民不
相易業若以為商賈之田則工亦當有田
===
矣賓客屬於秋官者盖諸侯朝覲會同之
禮畢則降而肉袒請刑屬之司寇所以威
懷諸侯矣玉府共王之獨用內府待邦之
大用亦猶古有世藏而豈以斂之四方乎
三公北面執璧后致飲而降醫酏原其禮
意自備而豈謂不與尊敵乎內小臣之掌
盖親族之在四方昏姻之所往來固以君

translation_en:
…promote the capable and bring them into office to govern them; yet even then, they never demanded perfection. How could this resemble later ages, when men were selected for office on the strength of reputation, while their conduct and accomplishments went unheard of? Assembling the people to read the laws was no harassment. The closer the relationship with the people, the more frequent the instruction, and thus the people advanced daily toward goodness. The five monetary levies administered by the Market Shop Officer were no harsh exaction. They restrained people’s pursuit of secondary occupations and encouraged devotion to the fundamental occupation of agriculture, so that frivolity and deceit among the people disappeared of themselves. Interest was paid in the products due as service to the state: farmers, for example, supplied grain, and artisans supplied implements. Payment was made convenient by accepting whatever people possessed. This was not lending money to exact repayment; how, then, could it constitute pursuit of profit? The commercial land administered by the Land Allotment Officer was presumably land that officials sold on behalf of the government, rather than land allotted to merchants. The four occupational groups did not exchange occupations. If this were taken to mean land assigned to merchants, artisans too would have to possess land.

Guests came under the Ministry of Autumn because, when the feudal lords had completed the rites of court audiences and assemblies, they descended, bared their upper bodies, and submitted themselves for punishment. Placing them under the Minister of Justice served both to overawe the feudal lords and to win their allegiance. The Jade Treasury supplied the king’s personal needs, while the Inner Treasury provided for the state’s major expenditures. This likewise resembled the hereditary stores of antiquity: how could it mean exacting wealth from all quarters? The Three Dukes faced north holding jade discs; the queen presented drink and bestowed yi and ye beverages. Examining the intent of these rites reveals that their provisions were complete in themselves. How could one say that they did not stand as equals in honor [?]? The duties of the Inner Junior Servitor concerned royal relatives living in the various regions and exchanges with relatives by marriage. These were certainly carried out by the ruler’s command and did not constitute private dealings with outside powers. The distinctions made by the Marriage Mediator concerned men and women marrying at the proper time: a woman taken in formal marriage became a wife, while one who eloped became a concubine. This followed the gradations of ritual □…

…unrestrained disorder. The sage took thought for all under Heaven, established regulations for every matter, and provided safeguards for every particular. Nothing went unexamined; no affair lacked meticulous provision. Lin Xiaocun’s attacks in his Ten Discourses and Ten Objections, and He Xiu’s denunciation of the book as a conspiracy of the Six States, cannot blemish this book. They merely bring upon their authors the guilt of insulting the sage. Among those in later ages who put it into practice, the usurper Wang Mang of the Xin dynasty was one whom ritual principles necessarily condemned to execution. As for the obstinately misguided Wang Anshi, he had already gravely misconstrued the institutional design of the Grand Steward. What is regrettable is that, although Wang Tong cherished it deeply, his age had no ruler intent on good government; and although Emperor Taizong of the Tang believed in it profoundly, his ministers lacked the ability to assist a true king. Alas! Was this the misfortune of the Rites of Zhou? Perhaps Heaven did not yet wish these people to receive the blessings of good government!

If one insists that Mencius had not seen it and asks how Han scholars could have brought it to prominence, then the feudal lords’ destruction of the records was not as ruthless as the Qin burning of books, and the Five Classics [four illegible characters; sense uncertain]. 未甞不以周禮為聖人之經故其言曰周
禮一書廣大精密周家法度在焉但

上遇文武之君始得行其志斯言也愚甞

諸儒之疑，吾甞於朱子而取衷矣。其語錄所載，師友之講劇、門人之論著，不一而足，未甞不以周禮為聖人之經。故其言曰：「周禮一書，廣大精密，周家法度在焉。但未敢令初學者看，學有先後耳。」又曰：「理會周禮，非位至宰相不能行；若至宰相，亦須上遇文武之君，始得行其志。」斯言也，愚甞三復之矣，可以破羣疑而一衆志者乎？學而躐進，終無所得；苟非其人，道不虛行。故疑周禮者，欲學而未知聖人之心者也；行周禮者，有志而未得聖人之心者也。

translation_en:
…As for the doubts of the various scholars, I have sought a balanced judgment in Master Zhu. His recorded sayings contain discussions [?] among teachers and friends, and there are numerous writings by his disciples; throughout, the Rites of Zhou is treated as a classic of the sage. Thus he said: “The Rites of Zhou is comprehensive and precise; the laws and institutions of the Zhou house are contained in it. I have simply not ventured to let beginners read it, for learning has its proper sequence.” He also said: “To understand and put the Rites of Zhou into practice, one must attain the position of chief councilor. Even then, one must serve a ruler like King Wen or King Wu before one can carry out one’s aspirations.” I have repeatedly pondered these words. Could they not dispel the many doubts and unite people’s purposes? If one skips stages in learning, one ultimately gains nothing; without the right person, the Way cannot put itself into practice. Thus those who doubt the Rites of Zhou wish to learn but do not yet understand the sage’s mind; those who would put it into practice have the ambition but have not yet grasped the sage’s mind.
Our imperial ancestors consulted antiquity in establishing offices, drawing extensively upon the Rites of Zhou. Today the Three Dukes and Three Junior Guardians stand alongside one another, while the Six Ministers divide their duties; the palace and the government offices sustain one another, while the inner and outer administrations check one another. The provisions governing these arrangements in the Ancestral Injunctions are very detailed, and those set out in the official system can be examined. Now, with a sagely and enlightened Son of Heaven above and worthy ministers assisting in government below, this is precisely the time to put them into practice. If we take their intent as our guide without clinging to their outward forms, and further seek out and attend to the Duke of Zhou’s profound wisdom and far-reaching deliberations, then the transforming achievements of the Zhou house can indeed be realized today. title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
辨天下之人者存乎智用天下之材者存
乎公夫不患人之難知患吾心之有未明
不患才之不足患吾心之有未公明則不
欺於人公則無累於己此古之人所以善
於取才而足以成天下之務者乎甚矣知
人之難也庸違象恭堯之所嘆巧令孔壬
禹之所憂秉之外雖杆拙而內實不欺迹
若可遺而志有足諒列是數者紛於吾前
而吾不能先立所主亦隨衆好惡而因時
===
異同於是賢不肖始混淆而無辨矣將合
己以為賢則小人側媚或以中其欲將附
己以為私則小人機阱或易至於離是故
以惠卿之儉邪而介甫信之則熈豐新法
之變固有自也以楊畏之詭秘而大防引
之則紹聖羣奸之禍不可悔也吾惟摯吾
智焉操吾公焉則如賈誼王褒之文學辛
湯段會宗之政事孰非才乎雋不疑之經
義暴勝之之高潔孰不可用乎是故郡守
