punctuated: 辨天下之人者存乎智，用天下之材者存乎公。夫不患人之難知，患吾心之有未明；不患才之不足，患吾心之有未公。明則不欺於人，公則無累於己。此古之人所以善於取才而足以成天下之務者乎！甚矣，知人之難也！庸違象恭，堯之所嘆；巧令孔壬，禹之所憂。秉之外雖杆拙而內實不欺，迹若可遺而志有足諒。列是數者，紛於吾前，而吾不能先立所主，亦隨衆好惡而因時異同，於是賢不肖始混淆而無辨矣。將合己以為賢，則小人側媚或以中其欲；將附己以為私，則小人機阱或易至於離。是故以惠卿之儉邪而介甫信之，則熈豐新法之變固有自也；以楊畏之詭秘而大防引之，則紹聖羣奸之禍不可悔也。吾惟摯吾智焉，操吾公焉，則如賈誼、王褒之文學，辛湯、段會宗之政事，孰非才乎？雋不疑之經義，暴勝之之高潔，孰不可用乎？是故郡守
translation_en:
Discerning the people of the realm depends on wisdom; employing the talents of the realm depends on impartiality. We should worry not that people are difficult to understand, but that our own minds lack clarity; not that talent is insufficient, but that our own minds lack impartiality. With clarity, we will not be deceived by others; with impartiality, we will not encumber ourselves. Was this not how the ancients became adept at selecting talent and thereby capable of accomplishing the affairs of the realm? How difficult it is to know people! Those whose conduct was disobedient but whose appearance was respectful were what Yao lamented; those with artful words and ingratiating manners, deeply treacherous, were what Yu feared. Others may be awkward in their outward bearing [?], yet inwardly free of deceit; their conduct may seem dismissible, yet their intentions deserve sympathetic understanding. When these several kinds crowd before us, if we cannot first establish a guiding principle, but merely follow the likes and dislikes of the multitude and shift our agreement or disagreement with the times, the worthy and unworthy become confused and indistinguishable. If we take agreement with ourselves as evidence of worthiness, petty men may use obsequious flattery to satisfy our desires. If we take attachment to ourselves as evidence of self-interest, petty men may readily use their schemes and traps to bring about estrangement.

Thus, when Jiefu trusted Huiqing despite his apparent frugality and wickedness [?], the upheaval of the New Policies during the Xining and Yuanfeng eras certainly had its source. When Dafang advanced Yang Wei despite his deceitfulness and secrecy, regret could not undo the calamity wrought by the host of treacherous men during the Shaosheng era. If I only apply my wisdom [?] and hold fast to my impartiality, then among such men as Jia Yi and Wang Bao, with their literary learning, and Xin Tang [?] and Duan Huizong, with their administrative ability, who does not possess talent? With Jun Buyi’s understanding of the Classics and Bao Shengzhi’s lofty integrity, who could not be employed? Thus, commandery administrators…

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
公府皆可舉士直指金吾亦得薦賢而何
守節之不善後乆要之變其初之足慮哉
昔范文正攝教西監晏元獻出判西京問
其人物范以二舉子對則富文忠張文定
也說者謂一問荅之頃萃四相焉張忠定
守金陵遇殿直范延貴詢其所見范以張
希顏對即日並薦于朝說者謂一邂逅之
間獲二士焉夫文正取士以忠孝為大節
以不欺為根本忠定亦嘗言問君子得君
===
子問小人得小人則公與明者二公之素
定矣故得士之易其即堂下一言而知醙
明野中一見而知𡩋缺者乎彼一匡之功
天下賴矣而實出於窘辱備嘗之士澶淵
之役所謂危矣而奚嫌乎好剛使氣之疵
盖鮑叔牙有見於管仲足興覇圖而王旦
畢士安亦知西北跳梁非寇凖莫能制其
亦明而公矣故語其常惟大節之觀也語
於用惟才之宜也古人之應變從權有不

translation_en:
…the ducal offices could all nominate worthy men, and investigating censors and officers of the Imperial Insignia Guard could likewise recommend the able. Why, then, need one worry that men who uphold their integrity might fail to maintain it to the end, or that friends of long standing might abandon their original commitments?

Formerly, when Fan Wenzheng was provisionally overseeing instruction at the Western Directorate [?], Yan Yuanxian went out to administer the Western Capital and asked him about its men of talent. Fan named two examination candidates: Fu Wenzhong and Zhang Wending. Commentators said that four chief councilors were brought together in a single exchange of question and answer. When Zhang Zhongding governed Jinling, he encountered the Palace Attendant Fan Yangui and asked whom he had met. Fan named Zhang Xiyan, and that very day Zhang Zhongding recommended both men to the court. Commentators said that a single chance encounter had yielded two worthy men.

In selecting men, Wenzheng took loyalty and filial piety as the cardinal virtues, and freedom from deceit as the foundation. Zhongding, too, once said: “Ask a gentleman, and you obtain a gentleman; ask a petty man, and you obtain a petty man.” Impartiality and discernment were thus qualities long established in these two lords. Was their ease in finding worthy men like recognizing Souming [?; apparently Zongming] from a single utterance below the hall, or recognizing Ning Que [?; apparently Ji Que] from a single encounter in the fields?

All under Heaven benefited from that achievement of restoring order, yet it was accomplished by a man who had experienced every kind of hardship and humiliation. The campaign at Chanyuan was indeed perilous; why, then, object to the faults of a fondness for forcefulness and an impetuous temper? Bao Shuya perceived that Guan Zhong could establish the foundations of hegemony, while Wang Dan and Bi Shi’an likewise knew that none but Kou Zhun could subdue the marauders in the northwest. They, too, possessed discernment and impartiality.

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以一律拘者如此故過可用也孟明不見
廢於秦伯毀可用也陳平不見棄於魏無
知不然則濟河之師造漢之業其孰與成
哉雖然且有說也明揚之下士風係焉變
動之機世道由焉故俗敝易於尚同而毀
譽增於附和管氏所以短鮑叔而右隰朋
者豈無見乎故知人而明矣用人而公矣
若可盡矣而周天下之慮示轉移之妙廟
堂之上必自有斟酌者而非區區之愚所
===
能與也惟執事進而教之
第五問
程尚寧
同考試官學正錢批策問雖以漢言猶
有不足於漢之意子能發之而於時弊殽論剴
切區畫精當可以驗用世之志矣
同考試官主事秦批時弊一策正欲觀
士子才識此作歷舉漢事纖悉無遺至篇末通
變之術又皆鑿鑿可行是誠達於治體者莫謂

translation_en:
…not being bound by a single rule was like this. Thus a man may be employed despite his faults: Mengming was not dismissed by the Earl of Qin. A man may be employed despite slander: Chen Ping was not abandoned by Wei Wuzhi. Otherwise, with whose help could the expedition across the Yellow River and the founding of the Han have been accomplished? Nevertheless, there is something further to say. The discernment and promotion of worthy men affects the ethos of scholars; the pivotal moments of change determine the course of the age. When customs deteriorate, people readily prize conformity, and slander and praise multiply through the echoing of others’ opinions. Was Guan Zhong without insight when he found fault with Bao Shu and preferred Xi Peng? To discern men perceptively and employ them impartially might seem to exhaust the matter. Yet comprehensively considering the concerns of the realm and displaying subtle skill in redirecting affairs must involve deliberations of the highest court in which someone of my limited understanding cannot participate. I ask that you, sir, offer me further instruction.

text:
爲豪傑之士歟耶
考試官右諭德彭批裁酌時宜切於救弊
非識見素定而有志經世者不能也
考試官侍講學士張批時務人人能言類迂
腐不切此策斟酌低昂有可行者非豪傑也耶
善爲治者固不可無明作之功亦不可無
惇大之化蓋明作有功紀綱之所由正也
惇大成裕風俗之所由醇也紀綱正於上
風俗醇於下天下有不善治者乎然所以
===
致是者亦不過用人行政二者之間而已
執事發策以真西山所載漢治爲問若有
激于目前浮薄之習而思以矯之者愚惟
聖朝方建長策舉三代之隆區區漢治奚足擬
哉然明問所及亦不敢不對如文帝問田
叔長者叔乃舉孟舒張釋之問周勃張相
如上因止嗇夫不拜直不疑張歐處官世
以是予之龔遂有對宣帝說之皆用人以
長者爲言也何也懲秦之刻核世以爲忌

考試官右諭德彭批：裁酌時宜，切於救弊，非識見素定而有志經世者不能也。

考試官侍講學士張批：時務人人能言，類迂腐不切。此策斟酌低昂，有可行者，非豪傑也耶？

善爲治者，固不可無明作之功，亦不可無惇大之化。蓋明作有功，紀綱之所由正也；惇大成裕，風俗之所由醇也。紀綱正於上，風俗醇於下，天下有不善治者乎？然所以致是者，亦不過用人行政二者之間而已。執事發策，以真西山所載漢治爲問，若有激于目前浮薄之習而思以矯之者。愚惟聖朝方建長策，舉三代之隆，區區漢治奚足擬哉？然明問所及，亦不敢不對。如文帝問田叔長者，叔乃舉孟舒；張釋之問周勃、張相如，上因止嗇夫不拜；直不疑、張歐處官，世以是予之；龔遂有對，宣帝說之：皆用人以長者爲言也。何也？懲秦之刻核，世以爲忌而云然也。
translation_en:
…be a man of outstanding ability? [?]

Comment by Examiner Peng, Right Mentor: His weighing of present circumstances directly addresses the correction of abuses. Only someone with firmly established discernment and a commitment to ordering the world could achieve this.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: Everyone can discuss current affairs, but such discussions are generally pedantic and inapplicable. This policy essay weighs what should be diminished or increased and offers practicable proposals. Is its author not a man of outstanding ability?

Those skilled in governing certainly cannot dispense with the achievements of enlightened action, nor can they dispense with the transforming influence of generosity and magnanimity. Enlightened action produces achievements through which the governing order is set right; generosity and magnanimity bring about an ample ease through which customs become sound. When the governing order is correct above and customs are sound below, could the realm fail to be well governed? Yet the means of achieving this amount to no more than employing people and conducting government.

You gentlemen have issued a policy question concerning Han government as recorded by Zhen Xishan, seemingly moved by the shallow and frivolous habits of the present and wishing to correct them. In my humble judgment, our sagely dynasty is now establishing enduring policies and restoring the flourishing order of the Three Dynasties. How could the comparatively modest achievements of Han government bear comparison? Nevertheless, I dare not leave unanswered the matters raised in your discerning question.

For example, when Emperor Wen asked Tian Shu about men of mature virtue, Shu recommended Meng Shu. Zhang Shizhi asked about Zhou Bo and Zhang Xiangru, whereupon the emperor refrained from appointing the bailiff. Zhi Buyi and Zhang Ou were praised by their contemporaries for this quality in their conduct of office. Gong Sui gave a reply that pleased Emperor Xuan. All these examples speak of employing men of mature virtue. Why? Chastened by Qin’s harsh scrutiny, people regarded it as something to avoid, and therefore spoke in these terms.

translation_en:
…and thus they spoke in these terms. Yuan Ang spoke boldly and invoked the larger principles of government; Ji An did not bind himself to the letter of the law; Zhi Du was unbending and forthright in disputing right and wrong; and Bing Ji inquired why an ox was panting, earning the admiration of his subordinate clerks. In each case, their conduct was described in terms of attention to the larger principles. Why was this? Again, taking warning from Qin’s oppressive attention to petty details, people of the time valued this approach and spoke accordingly. Thus, in praising Han government, they said: “There was little outward embellishment and much substance, and the custom of mutual denunciation changed.” They said: “Everyone cherished his own good name and regarded breaking the law as a serious matter; they put righteous conduct first and submission to humiliation last.” They said: “Officials were secure in their posts, and the people took pleasure in their occupations.” Yet viewed from the present, prevailing customs were still shallow and vicious, as in the matters over which Jia Yi declared that he must sigh deeply. Officials, moreover, practised deception, as when Wang Cheng received a reward for a falsely inflated increase. How, then, could all these praises have been entirely justified? Although Emperor Wen’s age pursued leniency and generosity, the framework of discipline and order was perhaps not fully strengthened; although Emperor Xuan’s age pursued comprehensive scrutiny, customs perhaps gradually deteriorated. Thus neither of these two approaches can properly be neglected in favor of the other.
Our dynasty has built upon its achievements for nearly a hundred and sixty years. Laws long in force inevitably become lax, and things worn down develop defects: this is the ordinary course of affairs. Among those now serving in prefectures and counties, can it be said that there are none who turn swords into implements of husbandry and attend to agriculture, the fundamental occupation? Such men exist, but they may not necessarily be recommended for advancement. Yet everywhere there are men who are dilatory toward those below and zealous toward those above, pursue private interests and neglect public duties, practise elaborate flattery to purchase praise, and attend meticulously to registers and documents to display their competence. Among those who wear the robes and caps of office, can it be said that there are none who are ashamed to speak of others’ faults and refuse to bow before powerful favorites? Such men exist, but they may not have won trust. Yet there are those who devise slanders, busy themselves with gifts and bribes, seek audiences with princes and dukes to sell their services, and diligently perform their official duties while…

□知者亦有矣禮式有禁誣越有刑所以
律民者至嚴也然好相仇訐或流言道路
如司馬文正所疏小者及縉紳大者及公
卿矣冠履之分漸可長乎制以將領優之
廩餼所以治軍者甚密也然少有不副遂
譟呼轅門如蘇文忠所論其始在邊鎮今
且在畿甸矣肘腋之虞患可養乎為今之
計無亦振紀綱于上厲風俗于下用人以
長者非欲為姑息蓋革薄從忠反茲憸巧
===
之徒耳矣舉事以大體非欲為疎闊蓋略
細圖遠反茲因循之政耳矣必重循良而
久其任倣漢之增秩賜金唐之疏名坐臥
宋之帶銜京朝增郡守之權併監臨之法
疎其節目慎於黜陟若是而吏不稱未之
有也吏稱則俗化矣必獎廉靜而覈其實
如兩及門三上書必抑之同巷不見十年
不調必進之先器識後文藝布公誠舍私
昵若是而士不厲未之有也士厲則政行

punctuated: □知者亦有矣。禮式有禁，誣越有刑，所以律民者至嚴也。然好相仇訐，或流言道路，如司馬文正所疏，小者及縉紳，大者及公卿矣。冠履之分，漸可長乎？制以將領，優之廩餼，所以治軍者甚密也。然少有不副，遂譟呼轅門，如蘇文忠所論，其始在邊鎮，今且在畿甸矣。肘腋之虞，患可養乎？為今之計，無亦振紀綱于上，厲風俗于下。用人以長者，非欲為姑息，蓋革薄從忠，反茲憸巧之徒耳矣；舉事以大體，非欲為疎闊，蓋略細圖遠，反茲因循之政耳矣。必重循良而久其任，倣漢之增秩賜金、唐之疏名坐臥、宋之帶銜京朝，增郡守之權，併監臨之法，疎其節目，慎於黜陟。若是而吏不稱，未之有也。吏稱則俗化矣。必獎廉靜而覈其實，如兩及門、三上書，必抑之；同巷不見、十年不調，必進之。先器識，後文藝，布公誠，舍私昵。若是而士不厲，未之有也。士厲則政行
translation_en:
…there are also those who seek recognition [?]. Ritual regulations impose prohibitions, and false accusations and transgressions incur punishments: the means of regulating the people are exceedingly strict. Yet people delight in mutual recrimination and denunciation, or spread rumors along the roads. As Sima Wenzheng explained in his memorial, these reach the gentry in lesser cases and the highest ministers in greater ones. With the distinction between cap and shoe—between superior and inferior—at stake, can such a tendency be allowed to grow? Troops are controlled through commanders and generously provided with grain allowances: the arrangements for governing the army are exceedingly thorough. Yet at the slightest failure to satisfy them, they clamor at the camp gates. As Su Wenzhong discussed, this began in the frontier garrisons, but now has reached even the capital region. Can such danger close at hand be allowed to fester?

For the present, should we not invigorate discipline at the top and improve customs below? Employing mature and upright men does not mean seeking indulgent accommodation; it means abandoning meanness for loyalty and turning away from these crafty opportunists. Conducting affairs with regard to the larger whole does not mean seeking loose and impractical measures; it means passing over minutiae to plan for the long term and reversing this government of habitual inaction.

We must value conscientious, benevolent administrators and keep them long in office, following the Han practice of increasing their salary ranks and awarding gold, the Tang practice of inscribing their names where the emperor sat and rested, and the Song practice of granting them concurrent titles as capital and court officials. We should increase the authority of prefects, consolidate the arrangements for supervision, simplify their detailed regulations, and exercise care in dismissals and promotions. There has never been a case in which officials failed to discharge their duties under such conditions. When officials discharge their duties, popular customs are transformed.

We must reward integrity and restraint while examining their actual substance. Those who twice come to the gate or submit letters three times to seek advancement must be held back; those who live in the same lane yet do not present themselves, or go ten years without a transfer, must be advanced. Put capacity and judgment before literary accomplishment; act with impartiality and sincerity, and set aside private favorites. There has never been a case in which scholars failed to exert themselves under such conditions. When scholars exert themselves, government measures are carried out…

punctuated:
矣。於民則降典以折刑，明刑以弼敎，嚴等列，崇體貌，如賈生所謂「豫遠不敬」；辨等威，明物采，如程子所謂「禮險之大用」，庶其塞告訐之門乎？於兵則覈屯田以實儲蓄，練民兵以省浮冗。主餉必公，如寇潁川之迎賈復、張益州之給屯軍；將閫必嚴，如韓魏公鎭北門戮犯縣令者、王德用帥定州禁喧廩庾者，庶其削跋扈之階乎？凡此皆在上者因勢輕重而變通之耳。
抑愚聞朱子有言：「紀綱之振，以宰執秉持而不敢失，臺諫補察而無所私，人主又以大公至正之心恭已於上而照臨之。賢者必上，不肖者必下，有功必賞，有罪必罰，則天下之人更相勸勉，去惡從善，而禮義之風、廉恥之俗變矣。」草茅之言，不識忌諱，惟執事擇焉。
translation_en:
… indeed. As for the people, promulgate statutes to adjudicate punishments and make punishments clear to support moral instruction. Enforce distinctions of rank and accord dignified treatment, as in Master Jia’s saying, “forestall disrespect”; distinguish the authority proper to each rank and clarify the insignia and colors appropriate to each, as in Master Cheng’s saying concerning “the great function of ritual barriers” [?]. Might this not close the door to malicious denunciations? As for the troops, scrutinize military agricultural colonies to replenish reserves, and train the militia to reduce superfluous personnel. Those in charge of provisions must be impartial, like Kou of Yingchuan receiving Jia Fu, and Zhang of Yizhou supplying the garrison troops. Military commanders must be strict, like Han, Duke of Wei, who, while guarding the northern gate, executed a man who had offended against a district magistrate, and Wang Deyong, who, commanding at Dingzhou, prohibited clamorous disturbances at the granaries. Might this not remove the means by which troops become overbearing and insubordinate? All this simply requires those in authority to adapt their measures to the relative gravity of circumstances.
Furthermore, I have heard Master Zhu say: “The restoration of discipline depends on chief councillors upholding it without daring to let it lapse, and on censors and remonstrance officials correcting deficiencies and scrutinizing affairs without partiality. The ruler, moreover, must preside reverently above with a mind of supreme impartiality and perfect rectitude, overseeing all. The worthy must be promoted, the unworthy demoted; merit must be rewarded, and guilt punished. Then the people throughout the realm will encourage one another, abandon evil, and follow goodness, and prevailing attitudes toward ritual propriety and righteousness, and customs concerning integrity and shame, will be transformed.” These are the words of a man of the countryside, ignorant of what it is forbidden to say. I ask only that you, honored examiners, select what is worthy in them.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the wuzi year of Jiajing [1528], the Record of the Yingtian Provincial Examination was completed. Your servant Chao had already written the opening pages; your servant Ze was charged with composing an account of the completed undertaking. I therefore read the compositions cut into the printing blocks and exclaimed: “How splendidly refined and abundant! Nothing could surpass them! The writings from the first session are precise yet plain, profound yet clear, vigorous and penetrating yet pure and correct. Surely these are writings that analyze principle! Those from the second session are sound and coherent, classical and conformable to standards, tactful and apt yet unimpeded and fluent. Surely these are writings that give fitting expression to affairs! Those from the third session are broad in learning yet exact, rich yet restrained, illuminating things and comprehending government. Surely these are writings for ordering the world!

“From where, then, does literary expression arise? Heaven has its patterns, displayed in its celestial phenomena; earth has its patterns, manifested in its forms. 天下而立定四海之民是故
亘古獨盛孔子曰周監於二

天地聖人所不能違也我

===

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以東之海陰陽之會風雨之
交將不在兹乎百餘年來人
文充蔚甲於四方固
文明之化使然亦其所乗者然
也故觀夫江以北之人文其
氣廓廓爾其辭卓卓爾北方
之長材大器在焉觀夫江以
===
南之人文其氣烈烈爾其辭
燁燁爾南方之奇珍麗藻在
焉天下之文具體于是矣抑
諸士者其嘗求夫文之全體
矣乎夫言文者有與質並有
與行並有與禮並有與實並
不配質則本有不敦矣不孚

For more than a hundred years, cultural achievement has flourished here, surpassing that of all other regions. This is certainly the result of the civilizing influence of enlightened rule, but also of the natural conditions upon which it draws. Thus, when we consider the literary culture north of the Yangzi, its spirit is expansive and its expression outstanding: here are the North’s great talents and people of immense capacity. The literary culture of the whole realm finds its full embodiment here.

title: 嘉靖七年應天府鄉試錄
text:
行則言有不掩矣不約禮則
學有不至矣不副實則用有
不周矣若是者豈徒偏之爲
小雖謂之虚文可也孔子以
斯文自任豈是謂哉其將經
緯天地裁成化育彌綸萬變
而後可以言文之全體諸士
===
無亦於此是務乎天地流精
山川炳靈臻是人文造物之
始爲之也良亦勤止若顧以
虚文終之無乃不可乎故惓
惓於終篇也亦莫之敢以虚
文相告也
奉議大夫右春坊右諭德彭

…conduct, then one's words fail to be borne out; if learning is not regulated by ritual propriety, it falls short of full attainment; if literary accomplishment does not accord with substance, its application cannot be comprehensive. In such cases, is the fault merely the narrowness of partial attainment? One might even call it empty literary display. When Confucius took responsibility for “this cultural tradition,” could this have been what he meant? Only by ordering Heaven and Earth, bringing their transforming and nurturing powers to fulfillment, and comprehending the myriad changes can one speak of cultural accomplishment in its entirety. Should you gentlemen not devote yourselves to this?
Heaven and Earth pour forth their vital essence; mountains and rivers manifest their numinous powers, culminating in this human culture. In bringing it into being, the Creator has indeed labored diligently. If, instead, we bring it to an end in empty literary display, would that not be unacceptable? Thus I speak earnestly at the close of this piece, not daring to address you with empty literary display.
